<!-- page: index (md/index.md) -->
# Animux Guide

> Everything you need to make animation on Animux, from your first boot to a finished film.

<div class="hero" markdown="1">

# Animator freedom meets imagination

**Animux** is a free computer system for animators. Start it from a USB stick or in a virtual machine and you get one desktop with about a hundred ready programs for 3D, 2D, stop motion, video, sound and render farms. You install nothing and pay nothing.

This guide assumes you have **never used Linux**. Every step says what to click, and shows a screenshot where it helps.

<p class="buttons"><a class="btn primary" href="start/what-is-animux.md">Start here</a> <a class="btn" href="start/virtualbox.md">Try it in VirtualBox</a> <a class="btn" href="tutorials/first-3d-render.md">Make your first render</a></p>

</div>

![The Animux desktop. The Animux button at the top left opens the menu with all programs, and the dock at the bottom starts the file manager, terminal and web browser.](../images/desktop.webp)

## New here? Follow these five steps

1. **[What is Animux?](start/what-is-animux.md)**: what you get and what you need.
2. **[Try it safely in VirtualBox](start/virtualbox.md)**, or **[make a USB stick](start/usb-stick.md)** to start a real computer from it.
3. **[Take the desktop tour](desktop/tour.md)**: the menu, files and settings.
4. **[Run the self-test](help/self-test.md)** to check that everything works on your computer.
5. **[Make your first 3D render](tutorials/first-3d-render.md)** with Blender, then continue with the other tutorials.

When you like it, **[install Animux on the hard disk](start/install.md)** so your work and settings are kept.

## What do you want to make?

<div class="cards">
<a class="card" href="software/blender.md"><strong>3D animation</strong><span>Blender 5.2 with Cycles and EEVEE, plus characters from MakeHuman.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/pencil2d.md"><strong>Hand-drawn 2D</strong><span>Pencil2D, Krita and TupiTube for frame-by-frame drawing.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/synfig.md"><strong>Cut-out and vector 2D</strong><span>Synfig Studio: automatic in-betweens and bone rigs.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/stopmotion.md"><strong>Stop motion</strong><span>Clay, LEGO or paper, shot with a webcam.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/kdenlive.md"><strong>Edit the film</strong><span>Kdenlive: shots, music, titles, export to MP4.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/audio.md"><strong>Sound and music</strong><span>Audacity, Ardour, LMMS and more.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/renderers.md"><strong>Rendering</strong><span>Cycles, POV-Ray, LuxCore, Mitsuba, appleseed, pbrt.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="software/flamenco.md"><strong>Render farm</strong><span>Many computers rendering one film with Flamenco.</span></a>
</div>

## For programs and AI agents

This guide is also built for software. On Animux the guide is in `/usr/share/animux/docs` and is served at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`. Every page is also available as Markdown, and [llms.txt](../llms.txt), [a JSON index](../api/pages.json), [a software catalogue](../api/software.json), the `animux-docs` command and an MCP server come with it. See **[For AI agents](agents/overview.md)**.

<!-- page: start/what-is-animux (md/start/what-is-animux.md) -->
# What is Animux?

> A free, complete studio for animators on one disc image. What is inside, what you need and how you can use it.

Animux is an **operating system**, like Windows or macOS. It replaces or sits beside them and comes with the programs an animation studio needs. It is built on **Debian 12**, one of the oldest and most stable Linux systems, and uses the **Xfce** desktop, which is simple and light.

The current release is **Animux Genesis64 r16.3**. It comes as one file, `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso` (12 GB). The `_28` is the build number, not the release.

## What you get

| For | Main programs |
|---|---|
| 3D modelling and animation | [Blender 5.2](../software/blender.md), [MakeHuman II and MPFB](../software/makehuman.md), [FreeCAD, Wings 3D, MeshLab](../software/other-3d.md) |
| Rendering | Cycles and EEVEE in Blender, [POV-Ray, LuxCoreRender, Mitsuba, appleseed, pbrt](../software/renderers.md) |
| 2D animation | [Synfig Studio](../software/synfig.md), [Pencil2D and TupiTube](../software/pencil2d.md), [Krita](../software/krita.md) |
| Stop motion | [Stopmotion](../software/stopmotion.md) |
| Drawing and images | [Krita](../software/krita.md), [GIMP, Inkscape, MyPaint](../software/gimp-inkscape.md) |
| Video | [Kdenlive](../software/kdenlive.md), [OpenShot, Cinelerra-GG, Avidemux, HandBrake, FFmpeg, DJV](../software/video-tools.md) |
| Sound and music | [Audacity, Ardour, LMMS, Hydrogen, MuseScore](../software/audio.md) |
| Studio pipeline | [Gaffer](../software/gaffer.md), [OpenUSD, Alembic, OpenEXR, OpenColorIO](../software/pipeline-formats.md) |
| Render farm | [Flamenco](../software/flamenco.md) |
| AI (offline) | [Upscayl](../software/upscayl.md) (image upscaling), [Whisper, rembg, Ollama, ComfyUI, LTX](../software/ai-tools.md) (subtitles, background removal, chat models, Stable Diffusion, video API), [AI agents in Blender, GIMP, Krita and Inkscape](../software/ai-agents.md) (MCP) |

The [software list](../software/index.md) shows all of them.

Also included: a web browser (Firefox), office-style viewers, a [self-test](../help/self-test.md) that checks every renderer, sample scenes, and this guide.

## Three ways to use Animux

1. **In a virtual machine**: a pretend computer inside Windows, macOS or Linux. Nothing on your computer changes. It is the best way to look around. → [VirtualBox guide](virtualbox.md)
2. **Live from a USB stick**: start a real computer from the stick. It runs at full speed, and the hard disk is not touched. Anything you save inside the live system is **lost when you switch off**, unless you save it to a USB drive. → [USB stick guide](usb-stick.md)
3. **Installed on a disk**: Animux becomes a normal system, and your files and settings stay. → [Installation guide](install.md)

!!! tip "Not sure? Start with VirtualBox."
    A virtual machine is slower than a real computer, especially for 3D, but it is completely safe. When you like Animux, put it on a USB stick or install it.

## What your computer needs

| | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| Processor | 64-bit Intel or AMD, 2 cores | 4 or more cores, made in 2013 or later |
| Memory (RAM) | 4 GB | 16 GB or more |
| Disk space (to install) | 40 GB | 100 GB or more |
| USB stick (live use) | 16 GB | 32 GB, USB 3 |
| Graphics | any | a recent AMD, Intel or NVIDIA card |

!!! warning "Very old processors"
    Blender 5, appleseed, Mitsuba and LuxCoreRender need a processor with **SSE4.2**; Mitsuba and LuxCore also need **AVX**. Almost every Intel or AMD processor sold since about 2011 has both. On an older one these programs do not start; the [self-test](../help/self-test.md) tells you so. See [Requirements](requirements.md) for how to check.

## Is it really free?

Yes. Animux and almost all its programs are **free and open-source software**: you may use them for any purpose, including paid commercial work, copy them and share them. The work you make belongs to you. Each program has its own licence; see [Licences and credits](../about/licenses.md).

## Words you will meet

- **ISO file**: one file that contains a whole disc. You use it to make a USB stick or to start a virtual machine.
- **Live session**: Animux running from the USB stick or ISO, without being installed.
- **Render**: let the computer calculate the final picture or film from a 3D scene.
- **Terminal**: a window where you type commands. You rarely need it; this guide gives every command in full.

More in the [Glossary](../help/glossary.md).

Careful: these can erase data.">GParted and Disks</a><a class="chip" href="../software/system-tools.md" title="Run other systems inside Animux, or packaged services.">Virtual machines and containers</a><a class="chip" href="../desktop/add-software.md" title="Install newer versions of programs from Flathub (for example Krita, OBS Studio, OpenToonz).">Flatpak <small>1.14</small></a><a class="chip" href="../help/self-test.md" title="Checks in a few minutes that the renderers and main programs work on your computer, and saves every test picture.">Animux Self-Test <small>1.0</small></a><a class="chip" href="../help/self-test.md" title="Small example files for each renderer and format, to open and learn from.">Animux Sample Scenes <small>1.0</small></a><a class="chip" href="../agents/overview.md" title="This guide, offline. Debian supports each release for years (Debian 12 with security updates until June 2028), and Animux adds current creative software from its own repository.</span></div></div>


Point at a program to see what it does; a click opens its page where there is one. The [software list](../software/index.md) has every program with its command, and [Versions](../about/versions.md) has every version number.

# Used in film production

> Films and studios whose storyboards, textures, frame fixes, colour and 3D were made with programs that Animux ships, with the sources.

<div class="films">

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">2012 · Blender Foundation open movie</p>
<h2 class="film-title">Tears of Steel</h2>
<p class="made">Storyboards drawn in <a class="chip" href="../software/krita.md">Krita</a></p>
<p>The storyboards were drawn digitally in Krita by David Revoy, the film's concept artist. He described the workflow in his making-of article <em>Tears-of-Steel making-of: storyboard workflow</em> (28 February 2012).</p>
<p>The film itself was made with Blender and is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 licence, so anyone may study it.</p>
<p class="source">Source: David Revoy, davidrevoy.com/article113/digital-open-source-storyboard-workflow</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">1999 and 2002 · Rhythm &amp; Hues · Sony Pictures Imageworks</p>
<h2 class="film-title">Stuart Little and Stuart Little 2</h2>
<p class="made">Textures and frame fixes in Film Gimp, a version of <a class="chip" href="../software/gimp-inkscape.md">GIMP</a></p>
<p>Film Gimp was a branch of GIMP for film work (later renamed CinePaint). At Rhythm &amp; Hues it painted textures, made paint fixes to rendered frames, removed dust, rigs and wires, and painted mattes. <em>Stuart Little</em> is among the films it was used on.</p>
<p>Sony Pictures Imageworks continued with Film Gimp on <em>Stuart Little 2</em>.</p>
<p class="source">Source: Film Gimp project history, filmgimp.sourceforge.net/docs/history.html</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Since 1995 · Studio Ghibli</p>
<h2 class="film-title">Studio Ghibli films</h2>
<p class="made">Ink and paint, colour and compositing in Toonz, today <a class="chip" href="../software/opentoonz.md">OpenToonz</a></p>
<p>Studio Ghibli chose Toonz during <em>Princess Mononoke</em> (1995). Its own version, the Toonz Ghibli Edition, has been used for ink and paint, colour design and digital composition on most Ghibli titles since <em>The Secret World of Arrietty</em> (2010).</p>
<p>In 2016 Dwango released that software as open source: OpenToonz, which Animux builds and ships.</p>
<p class="source">Source: Animation World Network, "Open-Source Animation Production Software 'OpenToonz' Available March 26", 18 March 2016</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">2024 · Dream Well Studio, Latvia</p>
<h2 class="film-title">Flow</h2>
<p class="made">Made in <a class="chip" href="../software/blender.md">Blender</a>, rendered in EEVEE</p>
<p>Gints Zilbalodis's film about a cat in a flooded world was made by a small team entirely in Blender and rendered with EEVEE, Blender's real-time render engine. It won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature at the 97th Academy Awards on 2 March 2025, ahead of films from Pixar, DreamWorks and Aardman.</p>
<p>The director thanked Blender in his acceptance.</p>
<p class="source">Source: CDM, "How Latvia's Flow used open source Blender in Oscar animation win", March 2025</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Since 2019 · Ubisoft Animation Studio</p>
<h2 class="film-title">Ubisoft Animation Studio</h2>
<p class="made">Main 3D tool: <a class="chip" href="../software/blender.md">Blender</a></p>
<p>In July 2019 Ubisoft Animation Studio, the animation division of Ubisoft Film &amp; Television, adopted Blender as its main digital content creation tool, replacing its in-house software, and joined the Blender Development Fund as a gold member.</p>
<p>It also released Mixer, its tool for several artists working in one Blender scene at once, as open source.</p>
<p class="source">Source: Ubisoft News, "Ubisoft Joins Blender Development Fund to Support Open Source Animation", 22 July 2019</p>
</article>

</div>

Animux ships the current versions of these programs: Krita for storyboards and paintings, GIMP 3 for plates, textures and frame fixes, OpenToonz for 2D animation, Blender for 3D. See [Animux at a glance](at-a-glance.md) for all programs.

<!-- page: start/requirements (md/start/requirements.md) -->
# Computer requirements

> Check your processor, memory, disk and graphics card before you start, and learn what each one affects.

## Quick check

| Part | Minimum | Good | What it affects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Processor (CPU) | 64-bit, 2 cores, **SSE4.2** | 4–16 cores, **AVX2** | Render speed, simulations, video export |
| Memory (RAM) | 4 GB | 16–32 GB | How big your scenes can be. The live session also keeps its files in RAM. |
| Disk | 40 GB free | 100 GB+ on an SSD | Installing, project files, renders |
| Graphics card (GPU) | any that shows a picture | AMD Radeon or NVIDIA GeForce from the last 6 years | Smooth 3D views in Blender, Krita canvas speed, Upscayl |
| Screen | 1280 × 720 | 1920 × 1080 or larger | Blender and video editors need room |
| Network | not needed | wired or Wi-Fi | Updates, render farm |

## Does my processor have SSE4.2 and AVX?

Animux itself runs on any 64-bit PC. Four programs need newer processor features:

| Program | Needs |
|---|---|
| Blender 5.2 | SSE4.2 |
| appleseed | SSE4.2 |
| Mitsuba 3 | SSE4.2 and AVX |
| LuxCoreRender | SSE4.2 and AVX |

Intel Core processors from 2011 onwards ("2nd generation" Core i3/i5/i7, model numbers 2xxx and higher) and AMD processors from 2011 onwards (Bulldozer, Ryzen and all later ones) have both.

**On Windows**, find your processor name: press **Windows key + Pause**, or open **Settings → System → About**. Search the web for the name plus "AVX".

**On Animux** (live or installed), open the [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md) and type:

```
grep -o -w -E 'sse4_2|avx|avx2' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u
```

If you see `sse4_2` and `avx`, everything works.

!!! note "Virtual machines"
    A virtual machine shows the guest the host's processor features, except in some setups. **QEMU** uses a basic processor model unless you add `-cpu host`, and **VirtualBox** shows the guest the real processor. If Blender says "illegal instruction" in a VM, see [Troubleshooting](../help/troubleshooting.md#blender-or-a-renderer-does-not-start).

## Graphics cards

- **Intel and AMD** graphics work out of the box with the free drivers included in Animux.
- **NVIDIA** cards work with the free *nouveau* driver included in Animux. It is fine for the desktop but slow for 3D. The official NVIDIA driver is not on the ISO; on an installed system you can add it ([Adding software](../desktop/add-software.md#nvidia-driver)).
- **GPU rendering** (Cycles on the graphics card) needs the official NVIDIA driver (CUDA/OptiX) or AMD's ROCm (HIP). Without them, Cycles renders on the processor, which always works.

## Memory and the live session

In a live session, everything you create (and every program update) lives in memory until you switch off. With 4 GB of RAM you can work, but keep projects small, and save to a USB drive often. With 8 GB or more it is comfortable.

## Drawing tablets

Wacom, Huion, XP-Pen and other tablets are recognised as pen devices with pressure in Krita, GIMP, MyPaint and Blender. For tablet button setup you can install the `xserver-xorg-input-wacom` package on an installed system.


---
<!-- page: start/get-the-iso (md/start/get-the-iso.md) -->
# Get the ISO file

> Download Animux, check that the download is complete and undamaged, and know which file is the newest.

Animux comes as one **ISO file**, a copy of a whole disc in a single file. For release r16.3 it is:

| File | Size | Release |
|---|---|---|
| `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso` | about 12 GB | Genesis64 r16.3 |

The number after `deb_` counts the builds, not the releases. Always use the newest release named on the [News](../news/2026-10-30-r16-3-release.md) page.

## Download

Download the ISO from the Animux download page, or copy it from someone who already has it (a USB disk works fine; it is free to share). The file is large, so:

- use a wired connection or a good Wi-Fi signal;
- make sure the disk you save it to has **at least 15 GB free**;
- on a USB disk formatted as **FAT32**, files over 4 GB do not fit. Use **exFAT** or **NTFS**.

## Check the download (recommended)

A broken download causes strange errors later. Compare the file's **SHA-256 checksum** with the one published next to the download (a long string of 64 letters and digits).

**Windows** – open **PowerShell** (Start menu → type `powershell`) and type:

```
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "$HOME\Downloads\animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso"
```

**macOS** – open **Terminal**:

```
shasum -a 256 ~/Downloads/animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso
```

**Linux** (including Animux):

```
sha256sum ~/Downloads/animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso
```

The long string printed must match the published one exactly. If it does not, download again.

## Next step

- Try it in a virtual machine: [VirtualBox](virtualbox.md) or [other virtual machines](other-vms.md).
- Start a real computer from it: [Make a USB stick](usb-stick.md).


---
<!-- page: start/virtualbox (md/start/virtualbox.md) -->
# Try Animux in VirtualBox

> Create a virtual machine with its own 80 GB virtual disk, start Animux from the ISO file and, if you like, install it, all without touching your real computer.

A **virtual machine (VM)** is a pretend computer that runs in a window on your real computer. Animux inside it cannot see or change your files. **VirtualBox** is a free VM program for Windows, macOS (Intel) and Linux.

You need:

- the Animux ISO file (`animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso`, 12 GB). See [Get the ISO](get-the-iso.md).
- **VirtualBox 7** from <https://www.virtualbox.org/wiki/Downloads> ("Windows hosts", "macOS / Intel hosts" or your Linux system).
- about **100 GB free disk space** on the real computer (the ISO plus a virtual disk that grows up to 80 GB), and at least **8 GB RAM**.

!!! tip "Fast way: let a script do steps 2 to 4"
    On Windows you can download [create-animux-vm.ps1](../../files/create-animux-vm.ps1), right-click it and choose **Run with PowerShell**. It asks for the ISO file and creates the VM with exactly the settings below. Then continue at [step 5](#5-start-animux).

## 1. Install VirtualBox

Run the VirtualBox installer and accept the defaults. On Windows it may warn that the network will be briefly disconnected; that is normal. Start **Oracle VirtualBox** when it is done.

## 2. Create the virtual machine

Click **New** (the blue star). Fill in:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | `Animux` |
| Folder | where the VM files go. Pick a disk with 100 GB free (for example `D:\VMs`). |
| ISO Image | select `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso` |
| Type / Subtype / Version | **Linux** / **Debian** / **Debian (64-bit)** |
| Unattended installation | **off**. In VirtualBox 7.1 and later leave **Proceed with Unattended Installation** unticked; in 7.0 tick **Skip Unattended Installation**. Animux has its own installer, and VirtualBox's automatic installation does not work with it. |

Click **Next**.

## 3. Memory, processors and firmware

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Base Memory | **8192 MB** (8 GB); 4096 MB is the minimum | Programs and the live session live in memory |
| Processors | **4** (or half of your real cores) | Rendering uses every core |
| Enable EFI | **leave off** | Animux starts with both, but "off" (BIOS) is the setting tested most. Tick it only if you want to test UEFI. |

Click **Next**.

## 4. The virtual hard disk (storage)

Choose **Create a Virtual Hard Disk Now** and set the size to **80 GB**. Leave **Pre-allocate Full Size** unticked: the file then starts small and grows only as Animux uses it.

!!! note "Do I need the disk to try Animux?"
    No. The live session runs without one. You need the disk if you want to [install Animux](install.md) inside the VM so your work is kept.

Click **Next**, then **Finish**.

### Recommended settings

Select the new VM and click **Settings**:

| Page | Setting | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Display → Screen** | Video Memory | **128 MB** |
| | Graphics Controller | **VMSVGA** |
| | Enable 3D Acceleration | **off** |
| **System → Motherboard** | Boot Order | **Optical** first, then **Hard Disk** |
| **Network → Adapter 1** | Attached to | **NAT** (the default; gives internet access) |
| **Audio** | Enable Audio | on (default) |

Click **OK**.

## 5. Start Animux

Select the VM and click **Start**. After a few seconds you see the Animux boot menu:

![The Animux boot menu. Press Enter on the first entry, "Animator Workstation". If you do nothing, it starts by itself after a few seconds.](../../images/boot-menu.webp)

Press **Enter** on **Animux Genesis64 – Animator Workstation**. Some text scrolls past for a moment, then the desktop opens by itself (about a minute in a VM). You are logged in as the live user **user** (password `user`).

![Animux running in VirtualBox (1024 × 768 screen).](../../images/vbox-desktop.webp)

To learn what each boot menu entry does, see [The boot menu](boot-menu.md).

!!! info "Using the mouse and keyboard in the VM"
    Click inside the window to use Animux. If the mouse gets "caught", press the **Host key** (right **Ctrl** on Windows and Linux, left **⌘ Command** on Mac) to release it.

## 6. Check that everything works

Open the menu at the top left: **Animux → Animux Tools → Animux Self-Test**. After a few minutes it lists every test:

![The self-test in VirtualBox: 29 tests passed.](../../images/vbox-selftest.webp)

See [The self-test](../help/self-test.md) for what the results mean.

## 7. Install Animux on the virtual disk (optional)

In the live session, everything you do is lost when the VM is switched off. To keep your work, install Animux on the 80 GB virtual disk:

1. Restart the VM. In the boot menu choose **Install Animux Genesis64 to Disk**.
2. Follow the [installation guide](install.md). Choose **Erase disk**: inside the VM this erases only the empty virtual disk, never your real one.
3. When the installer says it is finished, close the VM (**File → Close → Power off the machine**).
4. In the VM's **Settings → Storage**, click the disc under **Controller: IDE** and choose **Remove Disk from Virtual Drive**, so that it starts from the virtual disk next time.
5. Click **Start**. Animux now starts from its disk and asks for the user name and password you chose.

## Screen size, copy and paste, shared folders

Animux does not include VirtualBox's **Guest Additions**, so the screen does not resize automatically with the window, and copy and paste between your computer and the VM do not work yet.

- **Change the screen size** inside Animux: **Animux → Settings → Display**, then choose a **Resolution** and click **Apply**.
- **Scale the window**: VirtualBox menu **View → Virtual Screen 1 → Scale to 200 %** (or press Host+C for scaled mode).
- **Move files** in and out: use a USB stick (VirtualBox menu **Devices → USB**, then choose the stick), a cloud drive in Firefox, or e-mail.

On an **installed** Animux you can add the Guest Additions yourself. Everything they need (compilers and kernel headers) is included, and it takes about five minutes:

1. VirtualBox menu **Devices → Insert Guest Additions CD image…** A disc icon **VBox_GAs_7…** appears on the Animux desktop.
2. **Double-click that disc icon** so Animux opens it. (It is not opened by itself; the next step fails with "No such file" until you do.)
3. Open a [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md) and type:
   ```
   sudo sh /media/$USER/VBox_GAs_*/VBoxLinuxAdditions.run
   ```
   Type your password. A second window opens and shows the progress (*Building the VirtualBox Guest Additions kernel modules…*). Wait until it says **Press Return to close this window**, then press **Enter** in it.
4. Allow yourself to use shared folders:
   ```
   sudo usermod -aG vboxsf $USER
   ```
5. **Restart** Animux (menu **Animux → Log Out → Restart**).

Afterwards:

- The Animux screen **follows the size of the VirtualBox window** (and full-screen mode, Host+F).
- **Devices → Shared Clipboard → Bidirectional**: copy and paste between Windows (or macOS) and Animux.
- **Devices → Shared Folders**: add a folder of your computer, tick **Auto-mount**. In Animux it appears as `/media/sf_<name>` (for example `/media/sf_Projects`) and in the file manager. Files can be read and written from both sides.
- **Devices → Drag and Drop** works too.

This was tested with VirtualBox 7.2.6 on an installed Animux r16 (screen resize, shared folder in both directions, clipboard in both directions).

!!! note "After a kernel update"
    The Guest Additions rebuild themselves for a new Linux kernel when Animux starts. If the screen stops following the window after an update, run step 3 again.

## Webcam for stop motion

With the free **VirtualBox Extension Pack** installed (same download page), the VirtualBox menu **Devices → Webcams** passes your webcam to Animux, where [Stopmotion](../software/stopmotion.md) can use it.

## If something goes wrong

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| "VT-x is disabled in the BIOS" or "AMD-V is disabled" | Switch on virtualisation (Intel VT-x / AMD-V / SVM) in your computer's BIOS/UEFI setup. |
| Black window after the splash | Restart and choose **Workstation (KMS / no nomodeset)**, or set the Graphics Controller to VMSVGA. |
| Very slow | Give the VM more memory and processors. Close other programs. 3D is always slower in a VM than on a real computer. |
| Blender or Mitsuba say "illegal instruction" | Your processor or VM hides SSE4.2/AVX. See [Requirements](requirements.md#does-my-processor-have-sse42-and-avx). |
| No sound | **Settings → Audio**: Host Audio Driver **Default**, Controller **Intel HD Audio**. In Animux check **Settings → PulseAudio Volume Control**. |

More in [Troubleshooting](../help/troubleshooting.md).

## Other virtual machine programs

Animux also runs in **QEMU/virt-manager**, **VMware Workstation Player**, **Parallels** (Intel Macs) and **Hyper-V**. See [Other virtual machines](other-vms.md).


---
<!-- page: start/other-vms (md/start/other-vms.md) -->
# Other virtual machines

> Settings for QEMU and virt-manager, VMware, Hyper-V and Parallels, and the one setting that matters most for 3D programs.

Any virtual machine program that can start a 64-bit Linux ISO can run Animux. Use the same sizes everywhere:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Guest type | Linux, Debian 12 64-bit |
| Memory | 8 GB (4 GB minimum) |
| Processors | 4 |
| Disk | 80 GB, growing ("thin", "dynamically allocated") |
| Firmware | BIOS or UEFI. **Secure Boot off.** |
| Graphics | the standard adapter; no 3D acceleration needed |
| CPU model | **pass through the host CPU** (see below) |

!!! warning "Pass through the processor"
    Blender 5, appleseed, Mitsuba and LuxCore need SSE4.2 and AVX. Some VM programs show the guest a basic processor without them. Choose "host-passthrough", "host" or "copy host CPU configuration".

## QEMU (command line)

```
qemu-img create -f qcow2 animux.qcow2 80G
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 8192 -smp 4 \
  -machine q35 -vga std -nic user,model=e1000 \
  -cdrom animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso -drive file=animux.qcow2,if=virtio \
  -boot d -usb -device usb-tablet
```

On Windows replace `-enable-kvm` with `-accel whpx,kernel-irqchip=off`, on macOS with `-accel hvf`. Add UEFI with `-bios /usr/share/ovmf/OVMF.fd` (Linux; path may differ).

## virt-manager (Linux, also included in Animux)

**File → New Virtual Machine → Local install media** → choose the ISO → operating system **Debian 12** → memory 8192, CPUs 4 → disk 80 GB → tick **Customize configuration before install** → **CPUs**: tick **Copy host CPU configuration (host-passthrough)** → **Begin Installation**.

## VMware Workstation Player / Fusion (Intel Mac)

**Create a New Virtual Machine** → **Installer disc image file (iso)** → guest **Linux, Debian 12.x 64-bit** → disk 80 GB, *store as a single file* → **Customize Hardware**: memory 8 GB, 4 processors. VMware passes the CPU through by default.

## Hyper-V (Windows Pro)

Create a **Generation 2** VM with 8192 MB startup memory (untick *Dynamic Memory*), connect it to the *Default Switch*, create an 80 GB disk and choose the ISO. Then in **Settings → Security** **untick Enable Secure Boot**, and in **Processor** set 4 virtual processors.

## Apple Silicon Macs (M1–M4)

Animux is built for Intel/AMD (x86-64) processors. On an Apple Silicon Mac it can only run through emulation (UTM in "Emulate" mode), which is far too slow for animation work. Use a PC instead.


---
<!-- page: start/usb-stick (md/start/usb-stick.md) -->
# Make a bootable USB stick

> Step by step - write the Animux ISO to a USB stick with Rufus, balenaEtcher or Ventoy, start a computer from it, and fix the usual problems.

From a USB stick, Animux runs **at full speed** on your real computer and uses its real graphics card, without changing anything on the hard disk. Making the stick takes about half an hour, most of it waiting.

## Before you start

- **A USB stick of 16 GB or more.** The ISO file is 12 GB. A USB 3 stick (often blue inside the plug) is much faster, both to write and to run from.
- **Everything on the stick is erased.** Copy anything you want to keep onto your computer first.
- **Unplug other USB drives and memory cards**, so you cannot pick the wrong one by mistake.
- **The ISO file** `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso` ([Get the ISO](get-the-iso.md)).

!!! tip "Optional: check the ISO is not damaged"
    A download that broke halfway gives a stick that does not start. On Windows, open **PowerShell** (right-click the Start button → *Terminal*) and type, with your own path:

    ```
    Get-FileHash "C:\Users\you\Downloads\animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso" -Algorithm SHA256
    ```

    Compare the long code with the SHA-256 published next to the download. On macOS use `shasum -a 256 file.iso`, on Linux `sha256sum file.iso`.

Pick **one** of the three programs below. On Windows, Rufus is recommended.

## Option A: Rufus (Windows, recommended)

1. Download Rufus from <https://rufus.ie/>. The *Portable* version needs no installation. Start it and answer **Yes** when Windows asks for permission.
2. **Device**: choose your USB stick. Check the size, so you do not pick another disk.
3. **Boot selection**: click **SELECT** and choose `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso`.
4. Leave **Partition scheme**, **Target system** and everything else as Rufus fills it in.
5. Click **START**.
6. Rufus says **"ISOHybrid image detected"**. Choose **Write in DD Image mode** and click **OK**.
7. Confirm that the stick will be erased. Writing takes **10 to 30 minutes**.
8. When the bar says **READY**, click **CLOSE**.

!!! warning "DD Image mode is important"
    The ISO contains files bigger than 4 GB. The other choice, *ISO Image mode*, cannot copy them, and the stick then does not start.

!!! note "Windows says: You need to format the disk"
    After writing, Windows may say *You need to format the disk in drive E: before you can use it*. Click **Cancel**. This is normal: Windows cannot read the stick's Linux format. Formatting would erase Animux again.

## Option B: balenaEtcher (Windows, macOS, Linux, simplest)

1. Download balenaEtcher from <https://etcher.balena.io/>, install it and start it.
2. **Flash from file** → choose `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso`.
3. **Select target** → choose your USB stick. Check the size.
4. **Flash!** Wait until it says **Flash Complete** (10 to 30 minutes). Etcher checks the stick for errors by itself after writing.

On macOS, click **Ignore** if macOS says it cannot read the disk; on Windows click **Cancel** at the "format the disk" message, as above.

## Option C: Ventoy (several ISO files on one stick)

Ventoy is useful when you want to keep several builds or other systems on the same stick.

1. Download Ventoy from <https://www.ventoy.net/>, unpack it and start `Ventoy2Disk.exe`.
2. Choose the stick and click **Install**. This erases the stick once.
3. Copy `animux-genesis64-deb_28.iso` onto the stick **like a normal file** (Explorer or Finder). Later versions can sit beside it.
4. When you start from the stick, Ventoy shows a list. Choose the Animux ISO, then **Boot in normal mode**.

## Start the computer from the stick

1. Plug the stick in and switch the computer on, or restart it.
2. Straight away, press the **boot menu key** a few times. It depends on the maker:

| Maker | Boot menu key |
|---|---|
| Acer, Asus (laptops), Dell, Lenovo (most), Toshiba | **F12** |
| Asus (desktops), MSI | **F8** or **F11** |
| HP | **F9** (or **Esc**, then F9) |
| Gigabyte, ASRock | **F12** or **F11** |
| Lenovo with a "Novo" button | press the small Novo button while off |
| Apple Mac (Intel) | hold **⌥ Option** while starting |

3. Choose the USB stick. It may be listed twice, once as **UEFI: …** and once without. Either works; UEFI is preferred.
4. The [Animux boot menu](boot-menu.md) appears. Press **Enter**. The desktop appears after one to three minutes.

!!! tip "From Windows 10 or 11, without a boot key"
    Hold **Shift** while you click **Start → Power → Restart**. In the blue menu choose **Use a device** and then your USB stick.

Apple Macs with an M1, M2 or later chip (Apple silicon) cannot start Animux; use a [virtual machine](other-vms.md) there.

## If it does not start

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| The stick is not in the boot menu | Use a USB port directly on the computer (not a hub or front port). Write the stick again; with Rufus, check you chose **DD Image mode**. |
| "Secure Boot violation", or the computer skips the stick | Open the firmware setup (usually **F2** or **Del** right after switching on), set **Secure Boot** to **Disabled**, save and restart. You can enable it again later. |
| The screen stays black after the boot menu | Wait two minutes. Still black: restart and choose **Workstation (KMS / no nomodeset)** in the [boot menu](boot-menu.md). See also [Troubleshooting](../help/troubleshooting.md#black-screen-after-the-boot-menu). |
| Windows' disk is locked inside Animux | In Windows, turn off **Fast Startup**: Control Panel → Power Options → *Choose what the power buttons do* → untick *Turn on fast startup*. |
| Writing fails or stops halfway | Try another USB port or another stick. Cheap or old sticks often fail with files this big. |

## Saving your work in the live session

The live session forgets everything when you switch off. Save your projects to:

- a **second USB stick or disk**: it appears on the desktop and in the [file manager](../desktop/files.md) when you plug it in;
- the computer's own hard disk (it is visible in the file manager; be careful not to delete anything there);
- a cloud drive in Firefox.

To keep everything automatically, [install Animux](install.md).

## Using the stick as a normal stick again

The stick stays an Animux stick until you change it. To get it back for files:

- **Windows**: start Rufus, choose the stick, set **Boot selection** to **Non bootable** and click **START**. Or open *Disk Management* (right-click the Start button), delete every partition on the stick, then right-click the empty space → **New Simple Volume**.
- **macOS**: *Disk Utility* → choose the stick → **Erase** (format *ExFAT*).
- **Linux or Animux**: the *Disks* program → choose the stick → **Format Disk**.


---
<!-- page: start/boot-menu (md/start/boot-menu.md) -->
# The boot menu

> What each entry in the Animux start menu does, and which one to choose when the screen stays black.

When Animux starts from the ISO or USB stick you see this menu. Use the **arrow keys** to choose and **Enter** to start. If you press nothing, the first entry starts after 10 seconds.

![The Animux boot menu (GRUB).](../../images/boot-menu.webp)

| Entry | What it does | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Animator Workstation** | Starts the full desktop and logs in the live user automatically. | Normally. |
| **Render Farm Master** | Switches on the services a render farm head node uses: DHCP server and NFS file sharing. Starts to a text login without a desktop (in r16 it still showed the desktop). | Only on a computer that will hand out render jobs. See [Render farm roles](../software/flamenco.md#animux-render-farm-roles). |
| **Render Farm Slave** | A render node, started to a text login (in r16 still with the desktop). | Only on extra computers that only render. |
| **Install Animux Genesis64 to Disk** | Starts the desktop and opens the **installer** by itself. | To [install Animux](install.md). |
| **Workstation (KMS / no nomodeset)** | Desktop with the graphics card's own driver from the first second. | If the normal entry gives a **black screen** or a very low resolution on a real computer. |
| **Workstation (verbose / no Plymouth)** | Desktop, showing all start-up messages. | To see where starting hangs. |
| **DEBUG: Text Console** | Text login only (user `user`, password `user`). | Repairs and fault finding. |
| **Boot from first hard disk (EFI)** | Leaves Animux and starts the system on the hard disk. | Shown only on UEFI computers. |
| **GRUB command line** | The boot loader's command prompt. | Experts only. |

!!! tip "Black screen?"
    1. Wait two minutes. The first start in a VM or from a slow USB stick takes time.
    2. Restart and choose **Workstation (KMS / no nomodeset)**.
    3. Still black: choose **verbose** and look at the last lines, or see [Troubleshooting](../help/troubleshooting.md#black-screen-after-the-boot-menu).

## Adding your own options

Press **e** on an entry to edit it for one start. You can add words to the line that begins with `linux`, for example `toram` (copies the whole system into memory so you can remove the USB stick; needs 16 GB RAM or more). Press **Ctrl+X** or **F10** to start. Nothing is saved.

## After installation

An installed Animux has a shorter menu with Animux and its recovery mode. It shows the Animux splash screen while it starts and then the login screen:

![Animux starting from the hard disk.](../../images/boot-splash.webp)


---
<!-- page: start/live-session (md/start/live-session.md) -->
# The live session

> Animux running straight from the USB stick or ISO. The user name and password, what is kept, what is lost, and how to save work.

"Live" means Animux runs straight from the ISO or USB stick, without being installed. It is the full system with every program.

| | |
|---|---|
| User name | `user` (shown as **Animator**) |
| Password | `user` |
| Administrator (`sudo`) | allowed without a password |
| Computer name | `animux` |

You are logged in automatically. The password is only needed if a program asks for it, for example when the screen locks.

## What is kept and what is lost

!!! danger "Everything you save in the live session disappears when you switch off or restart."
    This includes files in the **Home** folder, settings, and programs you install. The system keeps them in **memory (RAM)**, which is also why big projects can fill the memory.

To keep your work:

1. Plug in a **USB stick or USB disk**. An icon appears on the desktop, and the drive is listed on the left in the [file manager](../desktop/files.md).
2. Save your project **directly onto that drive**, or copy it there before you switch off.
3. Before you pull the drive out, right-click its desktop icon and choose **Eject** (or **Unmount**), so that everything is really written.

Or [install Animux](install.md) so that everything stays.

## The disks of the computer

The computer's own disks appear in the file manager too. You can open files from them. **Be careful:** Animux can also change and delete files there. If Windows was not shut down completely (Fast Startup), its disk may be "read-only".

## Leaving the live session

**Animux menu → Log Out → Shut Down**. On a real computer, remove the USB stick when the screen goes black.


---
<!-- page: start/install (md/start/install.md) -->
# Install Animux on a disk

> Step-by-step through the installer, with screenshots, for a whole disk, a virtual disk or next to Windows.

Installing copies Animux onto a disk, so it starts without the USB stick and **keeps your files and settings**. It takes 15–40 minutes.

!!! danger "Back up first"
    Installing can erase a disk. Copy everything important from the computer to another drive first. In a [virtual machine](virtualbox.md) this does not matter: the installer only sees the empty virtual disk.

## Before you start

- A disk (or free space) of **at least 40 GB**; 100 GB or more is better.
- The computer plugged in to power.
- For **dual boot with Windows**: shrink Windows first, in Windows: **Disk Management → right-click C: → Shrink Volume**, and free at least 60 GB. Also turn off Windows *Fast Startup* and, if it is on, *BitLocker* for the time of the installation.

## 1. Start the installer

Start from the USB stick or ISO and choose **Install Animux Genesis64 to Disk** in the [boot menu](boot-menu.md). The desktop starts and the installer opens by itself.

(The installer can also be started from a normal live session: open a terminal and type `sudo -E calamares`.)

## 2. Welcome, location, keyboard

![The installer's first page. The steps are listed on the left.](../../images/install-welcome.webp)

- **Welcome**: choose your language, click **Next**.
- **Location**: click your region on the map, or choose region and city. This sets the clock and the date format.
- **Keyboard**: choose your keyboard layout. Type in the test box to check that the keys are right (especially `@`, `"` and `/`).

## 3. Partitions: where Animux goes

![Choosing the disk. In a virtual machine "Erase disk" only erases the virtual disk.](../../images/install-partitions.webp)

At the top, **Select storage device** shows the disk. Make sure it is the right one: check its size.

| Option | Use it when |
|---|---|
| **Erase disk** | The whole disk is for Animux (new disk, virtual machine). Everything on the disk is deleted. |
| **Install alongside** | Windows or another system is on the disk and you want to choose at every start. Drag the divider to give Animux its share. Only shown when there is room. |
| **Replace a partition** | You prepared an empty partition for Animux. |
| **Manual partitioning** | You know exactly which partitions you want. |

For **Erase disk** you can also choose **Swap** (extra memory on disk; *Swap (with Hibernate)* lets you hibernate) and tick **Encrypt system** to protect a laptop with a password at every start.

## 4. Users

![Your account: name, login name, computer name and password.](../../images/install-users.webp)

| Field | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| What is your name? | `Ada Lovelace` | shown on the login screen |
| Login name | `ada` | lower case, no spaces |
| Computer name | `ada-studio` | how the computer is called on the network; use different names on render farm computers |
| Password (twice) | | You need it to log in and to install software. Write it down. |
| Log in automatically | | Tick it only on a computer nobody else uses. |

## 5. Summary and installation

![The summary. Nothing has been changed yet; "Install" starts the real work.](../../images/install-summary.webp)

Read the summary. **Nothing has been changed yet.** Click **Install**, then **Install now**.

![Installing. A slideshow runs while the files are copied; this is the longest part.](../../images/install-progress.webp)

![Finished. Tick Restart now and click Done.](../../images/install-done.webp)

When it says **All done**, tick **Restart now** and click **Done**. Remove the USB stick when the screen goes black (in VirtualBox: remove the ISO under **Settings → Storage**).

## 6. First start from the disk

Animux shows its splash screen, then the login screen. Type your password and press **Enter**.

![The login screen of an installed Animux.](../../images/login.webp)

Continue with [First steps after installing](first-steps.md).

## Dual boot: choosing Windows or Animux

With **Install alongside**, every start shows a menu where you choose **Animux** or **Windows Boot Manager**. If Windows starts straight away without a menu, open your computer's boot menu (F12 etc., see [USB stick](usb-stick.md#start-the-computer-from-the-stick)) or set **debian** first in the firmware's boot order.


---
<!-- page: start/first-steps (md/start/first-steps.md) -->
# First steps after installing

> A ten-minute checklist for a freshly installed Animux, covering updates, the screen, the self-test, a project folder and backups.

1. **Log in** with the name and password you chose in the installer.
2. **Connect to the internet**: click the network icon at the top right (Wi-Fi) or plug in a cable.
3. **Update** the system. Open the [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md) and type:
   ```
   sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
   ```
4. **Screen**: **Settings → Display**. Set the resolution, and the position of a second monitor. See [Settings](../desktop/settings.md).
5. **Keyboard layout**: **Settings → Keyboard → Layout**, if the installer's choice is not right.
6. **Run the self-test**: **Animux Tools → Animux Self-Test**. Every line should say PASS. See [Self-test](../help/self-test.md).
7. **Graphics driver** (NVIDIA cards): install NVIDIA's driver for fast 3D. See [Adding software](../desktop/add-software.md#nvidia-driver).
8. **Make a projects folder**: `~/Projects`, with the [folder layout](../desktop/files.md#a-folder-layout-for-an-animation-project) studios use.
9. **Plan backups**: an external disk with a copy of `~/Projects`, and a **Timeshift** snapshot of the system (*Digital Asset Managers → Timeshift*).
10. **Make something**: start with [Your first 3D render](../tutorials/first-3d-render.md) or [Hand-drawn animation](../tutorials/hand-drawn-pencil2d.md).

## Differences from the live session

| | Live session | Installed |
|---|---|---|
| Files and settings | lost at shutdown | kept |
| Login | automatic as `user` | your own account and password |
| `sudo` | no password | your password |
| Start-up | text, then desktop | Animux splash screen, then login screen |
| Graphics driver | safe mode on BIOS computers | the card's own driver |
| Speed | depends on the USB stick | full disk speed |


---
<!-- page: desktop/tour (md/desktop/tour.md) -->
# Desktop tour

> The top panel, the Animux menu, the dock and the desktop icons, explained one by one.

Animux uses the **Xfce** desktop. If you know Windows, most things work the same way: windows, a menu, double-click to open, right-click for more options.

![The Animux desktop.](../../images/desktop.webp)

## The top panel

| Where | What | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Top left: **Animux** | The **menu** with every program | Click it, then move the mouse over a category. See [The Animux menu](menu.md). |
| Next to it | Open windows | Click a window's name to bring it to the front or hide it. |
| Middle right | Workspaces (four small boxes) | Four separate desktops. Click one to switch; handy to keep Blender on one and the browser on another. |
| Right | Network, volume, notifications | Click the network icon for Wi-Fi, the speaker for volume. |
| Right | Date and time | Click for a calendar. |
| Far right: **Animator** | Your user name | Log out, restart, shut down, lock the screen. |

## The dock (bottom)

| Icon | What it does |
|---|---|
| Blue rectangle | **Show desktop**: hides all windows (click again to bring them back). |
| Black box with `>_` | **Terminal**: type commands ([how](terminal.md)). |
| Grey filing drawer | **File manager**: your files and drives ([how](files.md)). |
| Blue globe | **Web browser** (Firefox). |
| Green rocket | **Application finder**: type a few letters of a program's name and press Enter. |
| Blue folder | **Folder menu**: shows the folders in your Home as a menu, so you can open one quickly. |

## Desktop icons

- **Trash**: deleted files go here first. Right-click → **Empty Trash** to delete them for good.
- **File System**: the whole system. You rarely need it.
- **Home**: your personal folder with Documents, Pictures, Videos and so on.
- USB sticks and disks appear here when you plug them in.

## Starting programs: three ways

1. **The menu**: Animux → category → program.
2. **Search**: press **Alt+F2** or click the green rocket, type for example `blender`, press **Enter**.
3. **Double-click a file**: a `.blend` file opens in Blender, a picture in the image viewer, a video in VLC.

## Windows

- Drag a window by its title bar. Double-click the title bar to make it fill the screen.
- The buttons at the top right of each window: **minimise** (_), **maximise** (□), **close** (×).
- **Alt+Tab** switches between windows.
- Drag a window to the left or right edge of the screen to give it half the screen.

## Shutting down

Click **Animator** at the top right (or **Animux → Log Out**) and choose **Shut Down** or **Restart**.

!!! warning "Live session"
    In the live session, files are lost when you shut down. See [The live session](../start/live-session.md).

## This guide on Animux

The guide is installed on Animux and works without internet: **Animux → Animux Tools → Animux Guide**. It also opens in the web browser at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`, and it opens by itself the first time you log in.

![This guide in Firefox on Animux (dark theme).](../../images/guide-home.webp)

<!-- page: desktop/menu (md/desktop/menu.md) -->
# The Animux menu

> A map of every menu category, so you know where to find the program for each job in an animation production.

Click **Animux** at the top left. The menu is sorted by **production job**, the way the original Animux was, not by program type.

![The menu with 3D Animation open: Modellers, Pipeline Tools, Renderers and Render Queue Managers.](../../images/menu-3d.webp)

| Category | Inside | Most useful |
|---|---|---|
| **2D Animation** | 2D animation programs | [Pencil2D](../software/pencil2d.md), [Synfig Studio](../software/synfig.md), TupiTube |
| **3D Animation → Modellers** | 3D modelling and character programs | [Blender](../software/blender.md), [MakeHuman 2](../software/makehuman.md), FreeCAD, Wings 3D, MeshLab |
| **3D Animation → Pipeline Tools** | Studio scene and format tools | [Gaffer](../software/gaffer.md), USD View |
| **3D Animation → Renderers** | Renderers with a window | POV-Ray, appleseed (others: see [Renderers](../software/renderers.md)) |
| **3D Animation → Render Queue Managers** | Render farm | [Flamenco Manager](../software/flamenco.md), Farmerjoe |
| **StopMotion Animation** | Frame-by-frame camera capture | [Stopmotion](../software/stopmotion.md) |
| **2D Graphics → Bitmap Editors** | Painting and photo editing | [Krita](../software/krita.md), [GIMP](../software/gimp-inkscape.md), MyPaint, mtPaint, GrafX2 |
| **2D Graphics → Vector Editors** | Drawing with shapes | [Inkscape](../software/gimp-inkscape.md) |
| **2D Graphics → Image Viewers** | Look at pictures and renders | Ristretto, Image Viewer, DJV |
| **2D Graphics → Ancillary Tools** | Other graphics tools | [Upscayl](../software/upscayl.md), colour calibration, scanning |
| **NLV Editors** | Video editing | [Kdenlive](../software/kdenlive.md), OpenShot, Cinelerra-GG, Avidemux |
| **DVD Authoring → Production** | Converting and finishing video | HandBrake, MKVToolNix, subtitle editors |
| **DVD Authoring → Backup** | Burning discs | K3b |
| **Sound Engineering** | Recording, music, audio setup | [Audacity, Ardour, LMMS, Hydrogen, MuseScore](../software/audio.md), QjackCtl, volume control |
| **Media Players** | Watch and listen | VLC, Parole |
| **Publishing** | Storyboards, PDF, print | [Scribus](../software/storyboard-publishing.md), PDF Arranger, Document Viewer |
| **Screen Casting** | Screenshots | Screenshot |
| **Digital Asset Managers** | Find and manage files and backups | File manager, Catfish search, Disk Usage Analyzer, Timeshift |
| **Animux Tools** | Animux's own tools | Animux Guide, Self-Test, Sample Scenes, Install DaVinci Resolve |
| Accessories, Education, Internet, Office, System, Settings | The usual desktop programs | Calculator, text editor, Firefox, Synaptic, Settings Manager |

!!! tip "Can't find a program?"
    Press **Alt+F2** and type part of its name, or use the [software list](../software/index.md), which says where each program is in the menu.

<!-- page: desktop/files (md/desktop/files.md) -->
# Files, folders and drives

> Where your work is stored, how to use the file manager, USB drives and network shares, and a sensible folder layout for animation projects.

## Your Home folder

Every user has a **Home** folder (`/home/your-login-name`, written `~` for short). It is like *My Documents* on Windows: everything of yours goes here.

| Folder | Use |
|---|---|
| `Desktop` | files shown on the desktop |
| `Documents` | scripts, notes, storyboards |
| `Pictures` | images, textures, renders (POV-Ray GUI saves to `Pictures/povray`) |
| `Videos` | finished films |
| `Music` | soundtracks |
| `Downloads` | what Firefox downloads |
| `animux-selftest` | results of the [self-test](../help/self-test.md) |

## The file manager

Click the **grey filing drawer** in the dock, or the **Home** icon on the desktop.

![The file manager (Thunar) showing the Animux sample scenes.](../../images/thunar.webp)

- **Left side**: places (Home, Desktop, Trash), drives and network.
- **Double-click** a file to open it; **right-click → Open With** to choose another program.
- **Copy and paste**: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V. **Rename**: F2. **Delete**: Delete key (goes to the Trash).
- **Show hidden files** (their names start with a dot, for example settings folders): **Ctrl+H**.
- **New folder**: right-click on empty space → **Create Folder**.
- **Open a terminal here**: right-click → **Open Terminal Here**.

## USB sticks and disks

Plug them in: an icon appears on the desktop and the drive is listed on the left in the file manager. **Always eject before unplugging**: right-click the drive → **Eject** (or **Safely Remove**), and wait until the icon disappears. Otherwise files can be damaged.

Drives formatted for Windows (NTFS, exFAT, FAT32) and Mac (exFAT) work. For drives used only with Linux, **ext4** is best; you can format a drive with **System → Disks** (this erases it).

## Network folders

In the file manager, click **Network** on the left, or type an address in the location bar (Ctrl+L):

| Kind | Address |
|---|---|
| Windows share / NAS | `smb://server-name/share` |
| Another Linux computer over SSH | `sftp://user@computer/home/user` |
| NFS (render farm) | `nfs://server/path` |

## A folder layout for an animation project

Studios keep every project in the same shape so everybody (and every render node) finds things. A simple version:

```
~/Projects/my-short/
├── 01-story/        script, storyboard (Scribus, Krita), animatic
├── 02-design/       character and set designs
├── 03-assets/       models, textures, rigs (.blend, .png, .exr)
├── 04-shots/        one .blend per shot: sh010.blend, sh020.blend …
├── 05-renders/      sh010/0001.png … one folder per shot
├── 06-sound/        dialogue, effects, music
└── 07-edit/         Kdenlive project and final MP4
```

- Use **lower-case names without spaces** (`sh010-walk.blend`, not `Shot 10 Walk.blend`). Command-line tools and render farms like them better.
- Use **relative paths** in Blender (*File → External Data → Make Paths Relative*) so the project still works when copied to another computer.

## Back up

Copy your project folder to an external drive regularly. On an installed system, **Timeshift** (*Digital Asset Managers → Timeshift*) can also snapshot the system before big changes. See [System tools](../software/system-tools.md).


---
<!-- page: desktop/terminal (md/desktop/terminal.md) -->
# The terminal, gently

> The twelve commands an animator actually needs, how to copy and paste them, and how sudo works.

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. You can do almost everything on Animux without it. It is useful for a few jobs: rendering in the background, converting many files at once, and fixing problems. This guide always gives the full command; you can copy and paste it.

Open it with the **`>_` icon** in the dock, or **Animux → Terminal Emulator**.

![A terminal running the Animux self-test.](../../images/vbox-selftest.webp)

## Copy and paste

| | In the terminal | Elsewhere |
|---|---|---|
| Copy | **Ctrl+Shift+C** | Ctrl+C |
| Paste | **Ctrl+Shift+V** (or the middle mouse button) | Ctrl+V |

Press **Enter** to run a command. **Ctrl+C** stops a running command. The **Up arrow** brings back the previous command. **Tab** completes file names.

## The twelve useful commands

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `ls` | list the files here | `ls ~/Pictures` |
| `cd` | go into a folder | `cd ~/Projects/my-short` |
| `pwd` | show where you are | `pwd` |
| `cp` | copy | `cp shot.blend shot-backup.blend` |
| `mv` | move or rename | `mv render.png final.png` |
| `mkdir` | make a folder | `mkdir -p ~/Projects/my-short/05-renders` |
| `rm` | delete for good (no Trash!) | `rm old-test.png` |
| `xdg-open` | open a file with its usual program | `xdg-open final.mp4` |
| `df -h` | how full the disks are | `df -h` |
| `free -h` | how much memory is used | `free -h` |
| `htop` | live list of running programs (q quits) | `htop` |
| `man` | the manual of a command (q quits) | `man ffmpeg` |

## Programs from the terminal

Every program in the menu can be started by name, for example `blender`, `krita` or `kdenlive`. Add `&` to keep using the terminal: `krita &`. The [software list](../software/index.md) shows each program's command.

Rendering without opening a window is the most useful trick:

```
blender -b ~/Projects/my-short/04-shots/sh010.blend -a
```

See [Command-line rendering](../tutorials/command-line-rendering.md).

## sudo: doing things as administrator

Installing software and changing the system need administrator rights. Put `sudo` in front:

```
sudo apt update
```

On an installed system it asks for **your** password (nothing appears while you type; that is normal). In the live session it does not ask.

!!! warning
    Only use `sudo` with commands you understand or that come from this guide. As administrator you can damage the system.

## Paths, quickly

- `~` is your Home folder; `~/Pictures` is the Pictures folder in it.
- `.` is "here", `..` is "one folder up".
- Names with spaces need quotes: `cd "~/My Projects"` – or avoid spaces.
- Upper and lower case are different: `Render.png` and `render.png` are two files.


---
<!-- page: desktop/settings (md/desktop/settings.md) -->
# Settings

> Screen resolution, several monitors, keyboard layout, mouse and tablet, sound, language, Wi-Fi, printers and power.

All settings are in **Animux → Settings → Settings Manager**.

![The Settings Manager.](../../images/settings.webp)

## Screen resolution and several monitors

**Settings → Display**. Choose the **Resolution** and click **Apply**; keep it if the picture is good (otherwise it returns after a few seconds). With two monitors, drag them into the right positions and choose which one is the **Primary Display**.

![Display settings.](../../images/display.webp)

!!! note "Only a few resolutions in a VM or on a new graphics card?"
    The normal start entry uses a simple, safe graphics mode on BIOS computers. Start with **Workstation (KMS / no nomodeset)** in the [boot menu](../start/boot-menu.md) to use the graphics card's own driver, which offers every resolution. An installed system uses the card's driver automatically.

**Colour accuracy** (for painting and grading): calibrate with a colorimeter and **DisplayCAL** (*2D Graphics → Ancillary Tools*).

## Keyboard layout

**Settings → Keyboard → Layout**: untick **Use system defaults**, click **+ Add** and choose your layout. Several layouts can be switched with the key combination chosen there.

## Mouse, touchpad and drawing tablet

**Settings → Mouse and Touchpad**: speed, left-handed buttons, tap-to-click. A three-button mouse is strongly recommended for Blender. On a laptop, tick *Emulate 3 Button Mouse* in Blender's preferences.

Drawing tablets work with pressure in Krita, GIMP, MyPaint and Blender. Set the pressure curve inside each program (Krita: *Settings → Configure Krita → Tablet settings*).

## Sound

The speaker icon in the panel changes the volume. **Sound Engineering → Sound Server Configuration → PulseAudio Volume Control** chooses which output (speakers, HDMI, headphones) and input (microphone) are used, per program. Audio for recording is explained in [Sound and music](../software/audio.md#how-audio-works-on-animux).

## Language, time and region

- Time zone: right-click the clock → **Properties**, or on an installed system run `sudo dpkg-reconfigure tzdata`.
- Language of the menus: on an installed system run `sudo dpkg-reconfigure locales`, choose your language (for example `de_DE.UTF-8`), then log out and in.

## Network and Wi-Fi

Click the **network icon** at the top right, choose the Wi-Fi network and type its password. **Edit Connections** there for fixed addresses (useful for render farm computers).

## Printers and scanners

**Settings → Print Settings** adds printers (most network printers are found automatically). Scanners work with **Simple Scan** (*Graphics → Document Scanner*).

## Power, screen saver and lock

**Settings → Power Manager**: when the screen turns off and when the computer sleeps. **Tip for long renders:** set *Put to sleep when inactive* to **Never** on the *System* tab, otherwise the computer may sleep in the middle of a render.

## Appearance

**Settings → Appearance** (theme, icons, fonts) and right-click the desktop → **Desktop Settings** for the wallpaper. Animux comes with its own wallpapers in `/usr/share/backgrounds/animux`.


---
<!-- page: desktop/add-software (md/desktop/add-software.md) -->
# Updates and adding software

> Keep Animux up to date and install more programs with Synaptic, apt or Flatpak, including DaVinci Resolve and the NVIDIA driver.

!!! note "Installed systems only"
    In the live session you can install software too, but it is gone after a restart.

## Updates

Animux gets software from two places:

1. **Debian 12**: security and bug-fix updates for the base system and most programs.
2. **The Animux repository**: Animux's own packages (Blender 5, Gaffer, the renderers, the menus, this guide…). It is signed with the *Animux Archive Signing Key*. **In r16 it is switched off** (`/etc/apt/sources.list.d/animux.sources`, `Enabled: no`) until it is online; Animux packages are then updated with the next release.

To update, open a [terminal](terminal.md) and type:

```
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
```

Answer **Y** when asked. Restart if the kernel was updated.

## Synaptic: install with a list

**System → Synaptic Package Manager**. Click **Search**, type a name (for example `natron` or `obs`), right-click the package → **Mark for Installation** → **Apply**.

## apt: install with one command

```
sudo apt install obs-studio
```

`apt search word` finds packages, `sudo apt remove name` removes one.

## Flatpak and Flathub: newer versions

Flathub has newer versions of many creative programs (Krita, OBS Studio, OpenToonz, Natron, Inkscape…). Set it up once:

```
flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists --user flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
```

Then install, for example OpenToonz (2D animation used by Studio Ghibli; already installed on Animux r16.3 and later):

```
flatpak install --user flathub io.github.OpenToonz
```

Flatpak programs appear in the menu after you log out and in.

## DaVinci Resolve

**Animux Tools → Install DaVinci Resolve** opens Blackmagic Design's download page. Resolve is free to download but not open source, so Animux cannot include it. It needs a strong NVIDIA or AMD graphics card with the vendor's driver.

## NVIDIA driver

For fast 3D and GPU rendering with an NVIDIA card, install NVIDIA's own driver from Debian's *non-free* section:

```
sudo apt install nvidia-driver firmware-misc-nonfree
```

Restart. Check with `nvidia-smi`. Cycles can then render on the GPU (*Blender → Edit → Preferences → System → CUDA or OptiX*).

!!! warning
    Do not install drivers downloaded as `.run` files from nvidia.com at the same time; use one or the other.

## What not to do

- Do not add software sources ("PPAs") made for **Ubuntu**; they can break Debian.
- Do not remove packages whose names start with `animux-` unless you know why: menus, branding and the start-up roles depend on them.

# Keyboard shortcuts

> A cheat sheet for the desktop and for the shortcuts animators use most in Blender, Krita, Pencil2D and Kdenlive.

## Desktop (Xfce)

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| **Alt+F2** | run a program by name |
| **Alt+Tab** | switch windows |
| **Alt+F4** | close the window |
| **Alt+F10** | maximise / restore the window |
| **Ctrl+Alt+D** | show the desktop |
| **Ctrl+Alt+T** | open a terminal |
| **Ctrl+Alt+L** | lock the screen |
| **Ctrl+Alt+Delete** | log out, restart or shut down |
| **Ctrl+Alt+← / →** | previous / next workspace |
| **Print** | screenshot (full screen); **Alt+Print** the window |
| **Ctrl+Esc** | open the program menu at the mouse pointer |

## Blender

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| Middle mouse drag | orbit the view; **Shift**+middle: pan; wheel: zoom |
| **Numpad 0** | look through the camera |
| **G / R / S** | grab (move), rotate, scale; then X, Y or Z to lock an axis |
| **Shift+A** | add an object |
| **Tab** | edit mode ↔ object mode |
| **I** | insert a keyframe |
| **Space** | play / stop the animation |
| **F12** | render the picture; **Ctrl+F12** render the animation |
| **N** | side panel (MPFB is a tab here) |
| **Ctrl+S** | save |
| **Ctrl+Z** | undo |
| **F3** | search for any command |

## Krita

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| **B** | brush; **E** toggles eraser mode |
| **[ / ]** | smaller / bigger brush |
| **Space**+drag | pan; **Ctrl+Space**+drag: zoom |
| **Insert** | new layer |
| **Ctrl+Z** | undo |

## Pencil2D

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| **N** pencil, **P** pen, **B** brush, **E** eraser, **K** paint bucket | tools |
| **, / .** | previous / next frame |
| **Enter** | play / stop |

## Kdenlive

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| **Space** | play / pause |
| **J / K / L** | backwards / pause / forwards |
| **I / O** | mark in / out point in the clip monitor |
| **Shift+R** | cut the clip at the playhead |
| **Ctrl+Enter** | render (export) |

<!-- page: software/index (md/software/index.md) -->
# All software

> Every program on Animux by job, with what it does and the command that starts it.

Animux has more than a hundred programs. This list has the ones that matter for animation, grouped by job. The name links to a longer page where there is one. **Start it** is what you type after **Alt+F2** or in a [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md); every program is also in the [menu](../desktop/menu.md).

!!! tip "Where to begin"
    New to animation software? Try these first: **[Pencil2D](pencil2d.md)** (drawing), **[Blender](blender.md)** (3D), **[Kdenlive](kdenlive.md)** (editing) and **[Audacity](audio.md)** (sound).


## 3D modelling and animation

Menu: **3D Animation → Modellers**.

| Program | What it does | Start it |
|---|---|---|
| [Blender](blender.md) | The complete 3D studio: modelling, sculpting, rigging, animation, simulation, rendering (Cycles and EEVEE), compositing and video editing. | `blender` |
| [MPFB (MakeHuman Plugin for Blender)](makehuman.md) | Creates realistic human characters, ready to animate, directly inside Blender. Switched on automatically. | `blender` |
| [Maya Workflow Kit for Blender](blender.md) | Makes Blender work like Autodesk Maya for animators trained on it: Maya hotkeys, marking menus, shelf, Channel Box and layout. Off until you switch it on. | `animux-blender-maya on` |
| [MakeHuman II](makehuman.md) | Stand-alone character creator: shape a human body with sliders, add clothes, a skeleton and poses, then export for Blender or games. | `makehuman2` |
| [FreeCAD](other-3d.md) | Precise CAD modelling for props, sets and objects that must have exact sizes. | `freecad` |
| [OpenSCAD](other-3d.md) | Build 3D objects by writing a short description instead of drawing them. | `openscad` |
| [Wings 3D](other-3d.md) | Small, friendly polygon modeller, good for learning how 3D meshes are built. | `wings3d` |
| [MeshLab](other-3d.md) | Clean up, repair and simplify 3D scans and heavy meshes. | `meshlab` |
| [Geomview](other-3d.md) | Viewer for mathematical 3D shapes (OFF files). | `geomview` |

## Renderers

Programs that turn a 3D scene into a picture. Menu: **3D Animation → Renderers** (several are command-line programs only).

| Program | What it does | Start it |
|---|---|---|
| [Cycles and EEVEE (inside Blender)](renderers.md) | Blender's own renderers. Cycles is realistic (path tracing); EEVEE is fast (real time). Start here. | `blender` |
| [POV-Ray](renderers.md) | Classic ray tracer: you describe the scene in a text file and POV-Ray draws it. The menu entry asks for a .pov file and shows the picture. | `animux-povray-gui` |
| [appleseed](renderers.md) | Physically based production renderer. Command line only on Animux (its editor window needs Python 2.7, which Debian 12 no longer has). | `appleseed.cli` |
| [LuxCoreRender](renderers.md) | Unbiased physically based renderer, good for realistic light, glass and caustics. Used from Python scripts. | `animux-vfx-python` |
| [Mitsuba 3](renderers.md) | Research renderer, also able to compute how a picture changes when the scene changes (differentiable rendering). | `mitsuba` |
| [pbrt-v4](renderers.md) | The renderer from the book "Physically Based Rendering". Ideal for learning how renderers work. | `pbrt` |

## Pipeline tools and file formats

For studios and advanced users: scene assembly, interchange formats and colour management. Menu: **3D Animation → Pipeline Tools**.

| Program | What it does | Start it |
|---|---|---|
| [Gaffer](gaffer.md) | Node-based tool for look development, lighting and scene assembly, used in film studios. Renders with Cycles. Includes Cortex, OSL, OpenUSD and Alembic tools. | `gaffer` |
| [OpenUSD tools (usdview, usdcat …)](pipeline-formats.md) | Universal Scene Description: the scene format shared by Blender, Houdini, Maya and game engines. usdview shows a USD file; usdcat, usdchecker, usdtree inspect and convert. | `usdview` |
| [Alembic tools (abcls, abctree …)](pipeline-formats.md) | Alembic stores baked animation (moving geometry) to move it between programs. | `abcls` |
| [Open Shading Language (oslc, oslinfo, testshade)](pipeline-formats.md) | Language for writing your own materials (shaders); works in Blender Cycles and Gaffer. | `oslc` |
| [OpenEXR and OpenImageIO tools](pipeline-formats.md) | EXR is the high-quality image format of film work (many layers, real light values). oiiotool converts, resizes and combines images; exrheader shows what is inside. | `oiiotool` |
| [OpenColorIO tools](pipeline-formats.md) | Colour management: keeps colours identical across Blender, Krita, Gaffer and your screen. | `ociocheck` |
| [OpenVDB tools](pipeline-formats.md) | Format for smoke, fire, clouds and other volumes. | `vdb_print` |
| [Animux VFX Python](pipeline-formats.md) | A ready Python 3.11 with Mitsuba, LuxCore, OpenUSD, OpenEXR, OpenColorIO, OpenImageIO, MaterialX and NumPy installed together. | `animux-vfx-python` |

## Render farm

Spread rendering over several computers. Menu: **3D Animation → Render Queue Managers**.

| Program | What it does | Start it |
|---|---|---|
| [Flamenco](flamenco.md) | Blender's official render farm: one Manager hands out frames, every other computer runs a Worker. Has a web page to watch the jobs. | `animux-flamenco-manager` |
| [Farmerjoe](flamenco.md) | The small Perl render farm that came with the original Animux. Kept for compatibility; use Flamenco for new work. | `farmerjoe` |

## 2D animation

Menu: **2D Animation**.

| Program | What it does | Start it |
|---|---|---|
| [OpenToonz](opentoonz.md) | The studio 2D animation program (the open-source Toonz used by Studio Ghibli): hand-drawn and cut-out animation with the Xsheet timesheet, scan cleanup, ink and paint, and a node-based FX schematic. | `opentoonz` |
| [Synfig Studio](synfig.md) | 2D vector animation with automatic in-between frames (tweening) and bone rigs for cut-out characters. | `synfigstudio` |
| [Pencil2D](pencil2d.md) | The simplest way to make hand-drawn, frame-by-frame animation with onion skin. Great first program for children and beginners. | `pencil2d` |
| [TupiTube (Tupi)](pencil2d.md) | 2D animation for schools and beginners: draw, tween and export short cartoons. | `tupi` |

## Stop motion

## AI tools

Programs that use machine learning. They run on your computer; nothing is sent to the internet.

| Program | What it does | Start it |
|---|---|---|

| [ComfyUI](ai-tools.md) | Stable Diffusion image generation with a node editor in the browser. Not on the ISO: install with sudo animux-install-local-ai --comfyui (--cuda for NVIDIA, --rocm for AMD). Models go in ~/ComfyUI/models/checkpoints. | `animux-comfyui` |
| [MCP servers (Blender, GIMP, Krita, Inkscape)](ai-agents.md) | Let an AI assistant work in Blender, GIMP 3.2, Krita 5.3 and Inkscape 1.4 through MCP: offline with a local Ollama model (animux-mcp agent) or with Claude Code. | `animux-mcp` |
| [LTX (Lightricks API)](ai-tools.md) | Video with sound from text or a picture, made in Lightricks' cloud with an API key (animux-ltx-api key). Also an MCP server for AI agents. | `animux-ltx-api` |
| [LTX-2 local (ComfyUI)](ai-tools.md) | LTX-2 video with sound on your own NVIDIA card (24-32 GB) in ComfyUI; about 40 GB of models. | `animux-ltx-models` |
| [Python for AI and data](../agents/command-reference.md) | Ready to run your own image and machine-learning scripts; use python3 -m venv for extra libraries. | `python3` |
