<!-- page: software/blender (md/software/blender.md) -->
# Blender

> The 3D studio at the heart of Animux. Blender 5.2 LTS with Cycles, EEVEE, Grease Pencil and the MPFB character add-on, and how to find your way around it.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Blender | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 3D Animation → Modellers → Blender |
| Version | 5.2.3 LTS |
| Command | `blender` |
| Good for | Beginner to professional |
| Files | .blend; imports/exports FBX, OBJ, glTF, USD, Alembic, STL, PLY, SVG |
| Licence | GPL-3.0-or-later |
| Website | [blender.org](https://www.blender.org/) |
| Self-test | `animux-selftest blender` |

</div>


Blender does almost everything in a 3D film: **modelling, sculpting, texturing, rigging, animation, physics (cloth, smoke, fluids), rendering, compositing and even video editing**. It is used for feature films, TV series, games and advertising. Animux includes the official **Blender 5.2.3 LTS** from blender.org ("LTS" = long-term support, with bug fixes until 2028), not the old Blender 3.4 that Debian 12 ships.

## Start Blender

**Animux → 3D Animation → Modellers → Blender**, or type `blender`. The first time, a welcome screen (the *splash*) appears; click anywhere outside it to close it.

![Blender's splash screen. "General" starts an empty 3D scene, "2D Animation" a Grease Pencil drawing, "Video Editing" the video editor.](../../images/blender-00-splash.webp)

## The screen

![The Blender window: the 3D viewport in the middle, the outliner (list of objects) at the top right, the properties editor below it and the timeline at the bottom.](../../images/blender-01-start.webp)

| Part | Where | What for |
|---|---|---|
| **Top bar** | top | menus (*File*, *Render*…) and **workspaces** (*Layout*, *Modeling*, *Animation*, *Shading*…): ready-made screen layouts for each job |
| **3D Viewport** | middle | your scene. Middle mouse button to orbit, wheel to zoom |
| **Toolbar** | left of the viewport | select, move, rotate, scale… |
| **Outliner** | top right | every object in the scene (camera, light, cube) |
| **Properties** | bottom right | settings, in tabs: render, output, object, modifiers, materials… |
| **Timeline** | bottom | frames, play button, keyframes |

## Your first hour

Follow the tutorials in order:

1. [Your first 3D render](../tutorials/first-3d-render.md): object, material, light, camera, render, save.
2. [A turntable animation](../tutorials/turntable-animation.md): keyframes and a video file.
3. [A character with MakeHuman](../tutorials/character-makehuman.md): a human with a skeleton, in Blender.
4. [From idea to finished film](../tutorials/short-film-workflow.md): how the steps fit together.

## Render engines

| Engine | Use it for | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| **EEVEE** | previews, stylised and cartoon looks, motion graphics | seconds per frame on a good graphics card |
| **Cycles** | realistic light, glass, reflections | seconds to minutes per frame |
| **Workbench** | quick clay previews | instant |

Choose in **Properties → Render → Render Engine**. On computers without a strong graphics card (and in virtual machines), **Cycles on the CPU** is the most reliable choice. EEVEE needs OpenGL 4.3; in a VM it runs through software emulation and is slow.

**GPU rendering in Cycles** needs NVIDIA's driver (CUDA/OptiX) or AMD's HIP. See [Adding software](../desktop/add-software.md#nvidia-driver), then **Edit → Preferences → System**.

## Grease Pencil: 2D inside Blender

**File → New → 2D Animation** gives a drawing canvas with layers, onion skin and a timeline. Draw with a tablet, animate frame by frame, and combine with 3D objects.

## Add-ons included

- **MPFB 2.0.18** (MakeHuman Plugin for Blender): the **MPFB** tab in the side panel (press **N** in the viewport) creates human characters. It is switched on automatically. See [MakeHuman and MPFB](makehuman.md).
- **Maya Workflow Kit 0.7.0** (new in r16.3, **off** until you switch it on): see [Coming from Maya](#coming-from-maya) below.
- Blender's own extensions (*Edit → Preferences → Get Extensions*) can be installed from extensions.blender.org when you are online.

## Coming from Maya

Trained on Autodesk Maya? The **Maya Workflow Kit** (by ohnsk, free, GPL-3.0) makes Blender work like Maya: Maya hotkeys and **Alt+mouse** navigation, **QWER** tools, the **Space** hotbox and marking menus, the **shelf**, the **Channel Box**, the **Outliner** with persp/top/front/side, the time slider and a Maya-style command line. It contains no Autodesk code.

It is installed but **off**, because it changes Blender's keys and layout. To switch it on:

1. Close Blender.
2. Menu **Animux Tools → Blender: Maya Workflow Kit on/off**, answer **y** (or type `animux-blender-maya on` in a [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md)).
3. Start Blender. The kit's welcome window says that nothing has changed yet; click **Make Blender feel like Maya**.

In Blender, the **Maya | Blender** switch at the top right (or **Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M**) changes between the Maya layout and Blender's own. To remove the kit from Blender completely, close Blender and run the menu entry again (or `animux-blender-maya off`). `animux-blender-maya status` says whether it is on.

The kit's help is in **Edit → Preferences → Add-ons → Maya Workflow Kit**. Blender tutorials and this guide use Blender's own keys: switch back with the **Maya | Blender** switch when you follow them.

## Rendering without opening Blender

Great for long renders, render farms and scripts:

```
blender -b shot.blend -a                          # whole animation, settings from the file
blender -b shot.blend -o //frames/f_#### -F PNG -s 1 -e 48 -a   # frames 1–48 as PNG
blender -b shot.blend -f 10                       # just frame 10
blender -b --python make_scene.py                 # run a Python script
```

`-b` (background) must come first. `//` means "next to the .blend file". See [Command-line rendering](../tutorials/command-line-rendering.md) and [Flamenco](flamenco.md) for many computers.

## Files

- Blender saves **.blend** files. **File → Save** (Ctrl+S). Blender keeps `.blend1` backups next to them.
- **File → Import / Export**: FBX, OBJ, glTF (games and the web), USD and Alembic (studio pipelines), STL (3D printing), SVG.
- Rendered pictures are not saved automatically: in the render window use **Image → Save As**.

## Learn more

- The official manual: <https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/5.2/> (also *Help → Manual*).
- Blender Studio's free courses: <https://studio.blender.org/training/>.
- The sample file `/usr/share/animux/samples/blender/turntable.py` builds a small scene by script.


---
<!-- page: software/makehuman (md/software/makehuman.md) -->
# MakeHuman II and MPFB

> Make realistic human characters with sliders, either in the stand-alone MakeHuman II or with the MPFB add-on directly inside Blender.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| MakeHuman II | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 3D Animation → Modellers → MakeHuman 2 |
| Version | 2.0.1 |
| Command | `makehuman2` |
| Good for | Beginner |
| Files | .mhm; exports GLB (glTF), OBJ, STL, MH2B (Blender), BVH (poses) |
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 |
| Website | [github.com/makehumancommunity/makehuman2](https://github.com/makehumancommunity/makehuman2) |
| Self-test | `animux-selftest apps` |

</div>


MakeHuman is the classic free character creator: you move **sliders** (age, gender, weight, height, face shape…) and get a clean, animation-ready human body. The project has two current tools, and Animux includes both:

| | MakeHuman II | MPFB |
|---|---|---|
| What | the stand-alone program | the same character system as a **Blender add-on** |
| Version on Animux | 2.0.1 ("Fantasy") | 2.0.18 |
| Start | *3D Animation → Modellers → MakeHuman 2* | in Blender: press **N** → tab **MPFB** |
| Best for | designing a character, exporting to games or other programs | characters you animate in Blender |

!!! note "About the name"
    The original **MakeHuman 1.x** (Python 2) is no longer developed. Its successor is **MakeHuman II** (`makehumancommunity/makehuman2` on GitHub). **MPFB** (*MakeHuman Plugin For Blender*) is maintained by the same community. Both use the same assets.

## MakeHuman II

![MakeHuman II. The two rows of icons at the top left choose the task (hold the mouse over an icon to see its name); the panel below changes with it. The character is in the viewport, with camera buttons on the right.](../../images/makehuman2.webp)

![The very first start: MakeHuman II asks where to keep your characters and downloads. Keep the suggestion and click Save.](../../images/makehuman2-setup.webp)

1. Start **MakeHuman 2**. The very first time, it asks for a **personal folder** (suggested: `~/makehuman2`); click **Save**. Then it shows **Base mesh :: selection**: keep **fantasy** (the MakeHuman II body; *hm08* is the classic MakeHuman 1 body) and click **Select**.
2. Click the **modify character** icon. The left side lists categories (**Modify character :: categories**) such as main proportions, head, torso, arms and legs. Open one and move its sliders: gender, age, muscle and weight change the whole body. The summary at the bottom right shows age, muscle, weight and height.
3. Use the other icons to add **clothes, hair, eyebrows, eyes**, a **skeleton** and a **pose** or expression.
4. Use the camera buttons on the right of the viewport to look from the front, side or top, or to fit the face.
5. **Save** the character as `.mhm` (a small file you can change later). **Export** as **GLB** (glTF, for games, the web and Blender), **OBJ**, **STL** (3D printing), **MH2B** (for Blender with the included *io_makehuman* add-on) or a pose/animation as **BVH**.

!!! tip "Small screen"
    Some MakeHuman II dialogs are taller than 800 pixels. On a small screen, move a dialog by holding **Alt** and dragging it with the mouse.

## MPFB inside Blender

![A human created with MPFB. The MPFB tab is the last vertical tab at the right edge of the side panel.](../../images/blender-08-mpfb.webp)

1. Start Blender, move the mouse over the 3D viewport and press **N**. Click the **MPFB** tab at the right edge.
2. Open **New human → From scratch** and click **Create human**.
3. Open **Model** and change the sliders, as in MakeHuman.
4. **Rigging → Standard rig → Add standard rig** (or **Rigify**) gives it a skeleton you can pose and animate.
5. **Apply assets** adds skin, eyes, eyebrows, hair and clothes from asset packs.

MPFB can also **load a .mhm file** saved by MakeHuman II (*New human → From save file*), or take the character straight from a running MakeHuman II (*New human → From MakeHuman*).

!!! info "Asset packs"
    MPFB and MakeHuman II include the base body and a few basic assets. Thousands of extra clothes, hair styles and skins (free, CC0 and CC-BY) can be downloaded from <http://www.makehumancommunity.org/> as *asset packs* and loaded with **MPFB → System and resources → Load pack from zip file**.

See the tutorial [A character with MakeHuman](../tutorials/character-makehuman.md).

## Licences of your characters

The program is AGPL-3.0, but **characters you export with the standard assets are yours to use, including commercially** (the base mesh and standard assets are CC0). Check the licence of extra community assets before you sell work.

<!-- page: software/other-3d (md/software/other-3d.md) -->
# FreeCAD, Wings 3D, MeshLab and OpenSCAD

> The other 3D modellers on Animux and when each one is the right tool next to Blender.

| Program | Use it when | Start |
|---|---|---|
| **FreeCAD** 0.20 | Props, sets and machines that need **exact measurements**, or parts for 3D printing. Parametric: change a number and the model updates. | `freecad` |
| **OpenSCAD** 2021.01 | You prefer to **describe** an object in a few lines of code (`cube`, `cylinder`, `difference`). Perfect for repeated parts. | `openscad` |
| **Wings 3D** 2.2 | You want a **small, simple polygon modeller** for low-poly models and learning box modelling. | `wings3d` |
| **MeshLab** 2020.09 | You need to **repair, clean or simplify** scans and heavy meshes (photogrammetry, 3D scanners). | `meshlab` |
| **Geomview** 1.9 | You view **mathematical surfaces** (OFF files). Mostly for teaching. | `geomview` |

All are in **3D Animation → Modellers**.

![FreeCAD's start page.](../../images/freecad.webp)

## Moving models into Blender

| From | Export as | In Blender |
|---|---|---|
| FreeCAD | **File → Export → OBJ** or STL (select the object first) | *File → Import → Wavefront (.obj)* |
| OpenSCAD | **File → Export → STL** (render with F6 first) | *File → Import → STL* |
| Wings 3D | **File → Export → glTF** or OBJ | *File → Import → glTF 2.0* |
| MeshLab | **File → Export Mesh As → PLY or OBJ** | *File → Import → Stanford PLY* |

Check the **scale** after importing: CAD programs work in millimetres, Blender in metres. Use the import dialog's *Scale* (0.001 for mm).

## OpenSCAD from the command line

```
openscad -o bracket.stl bracket.scad
```

![MeshLab.](../../images/meshlab.webp)

## Wings 3D

Wings 3D opens with an empty scene. **Right-click** in the grid to get the menu, for example *Cube*; select faces, edges or vertices with the four red cube buttons at the top and right-click again for the tools (Extrude, Bevel, Smooth …).

![Wings 3D 2.2.9 on Animux.](../../images/wings3d.webp)

!!! note "Wings 3D opens no window (r16 only)"
    Fixed in r16.1 (`_25`): the menu entry and the `wings3d` command start it safely. On Animux r16 (`_21` and earlier), Wings 3D opens **no window** on computers without a graphics-card OpenCL driver: the processor OpenCL driver breaks its start-up. Start it from a [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md) like this instead:

    ```
    OCL_ICD_VENDORS=/nonexistent wings3d
    ```

    The package `animux-menus` 1.0.17 fixes the menu entry (Wings 3D then always starts this way); see [Guide updates](../about/guide-updates.md#how-to-get-a-newer-guide) for installing a package file.

<!-- page: software/renderers (md/software/renderers.md) -->
# Renderers

> Cycles, EEVEE, POV-Ray, LuxCoreRender, Mitsuba 3, appleseed and pbrt-v4. What each one is good at, how to run its sample scene, and which one to choose.

A **renderer** calculates the final picture from a 3D scene: how light bounces, how glass bends it, how shadows fall. Animux has seven, from very easy to research-grade.

## Which one should I use?

| Renderer | Choose it when | How you use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Cycles** (in Blender) | Almost always: realistic, fast enough, in the program you model in | Blender → Render Engine: Cycles |
| **EEVEE** (in Blender) | Fast previews, cartoons, motion graphics | Blender → Render Engine: EEVEE |
| **POV-Ray** 3.7 | You like describing scenes in text; classic CG, maths art, teaching | menu *Renderers → POV-Ray*, or `povray` |
| **LuxCoreRender** 2.11 | Very realistic light: caustics, glass, interiors | Python scripts (`animux-vfx-python`) |
| **Mitsuba 3** 3.9 | Research, spectral rendering, inverse rendering | Python or `mitsuba scene.xml` |
| **appleseed** 2.1 beta | Production-style physically based rendering of `.appleseed` projects | menu *Renderers → appleseed*, or `appleseed.cli` |
| **pbrt-v4** | Learning how renderers work, with the book *Physically Based Rendering* | `pbrt scene.pbrt` |

All seven side by side, with full names and what each does best: [Renderer comparison](renderer-comparison.md).

Beginners: **use Cycles**, explained in [Blender](blender.md#render-engines) and the [first-render tutorial](../tutorials/first-3d-render.md).

!!! warning "Processor features"
    Cycles (Blender 5) and appleseed need SSE4.2; Mitsuba and LuxCore also need AVX. See [Requirements](../start/requirements.md#does-my-processor-have-sse42-and-avx).

## Try every renderer in two minutes

Each renderer has a sample scene in `/usr/share/animux/samples`. The [self-test](../help/self-test.md) renders all of them and saves the pictures in `~/animux-selftest/<date>/`:

```
animux-selftest povray blender mitsuba luxcore appleseed pbrt gaffer
```

These are the pictures the self-test made on Animux (in a virtual machine, a few seconds each):

<div class="gallery" markdown="1">

![Cycles (Blender 5.2): samples/blender/turntable.py](../../images/render-blender.webp)

![POV-Ray: samples/povray/animux-spheres.pov](../../images/render-povray.webp)

![LuxCoreRender: samples/luxcore/render.py](../../images/render-luxcore.webp)

![Mitsuba 3: samples/mitsuba/render.py](../../images/render-mitsuba.webp)

![appleseed: the helloworld example](../../images/render-appleseed.webp)

![pbrt-v4: samples/pbrt/animux-spheres.pbrt](../../images/render-pbrt.webp)

![Gaffer with Cycles: samples/gaffer/render.py](../../images/render-gaffer.webp)

![Synfig: frame 12 of samples/synfig/bouncing-ball.sif](../../images/render-synfig.webp)

</div>

## POV-Ray

POV-Ray reads a **text file** that describes the scene, and writes a picture.

```
#include "colors.inc"
camera { location <0, 2, -6> look_at <0, 1, 0> }
light_source { <-5, 10, -10> color White }
plane { y, 0 pigment { checker Gray White } }
sphere { <0, 1, 0>, 1 pigment { color Red } finish { phong 0.8 reflection 0.2 } }
```

Save that as `ball.pov`, then either choose **3D Animation → Renderers → POV-Ray** and pick the file (the picture opens by itself and is saved in `~/Pictures/povray/`), or type:

```
povray +Iball.pov +Oball.png +W1280 +H720 +A -D
```

`+A` turns on anti-aliasing (smooth edges), `-D` renders without a preview window. Hundreds of example scenes are in `/usr/share/povray-3.7/scenes`.

![POV-Ray asks for a scene file; the sample scenes folder opens first.](../../images/povray-gui.webp)

## LuxCoreRender

LuxCore is used here as a **Python module** in Animux's ready-made Python, `animux-vfx-python`:

```
animux-vfx-python /usr/share/animux/samples/luxcore/render.py ~/luxcore.png
```

Read `render.py` to see how a scene is described (camera, materials, lights) and how long it renders (a time or quality limit). LuxCore's Blender add-on (*BlendLuxCore*) is not included in r16.

!!! info
    On Animux LuxCore renders on the **processor**. It ignores the software OpenCL drivers that come with Debian, because they made it crash. On a computer with a real OpenCL GPU driver you can let it use the GPU by starting it with `ANIMUX_KEEP_ALL_OPENCL=1`.

## Mitsuba 3

```
mitsuba scene.xml -o out.exr
animux-vfx-python /usr/share/animux/samples/mitsuba/render.py ~/mitsuba.exr
```

Mitsuba writes **EXR** images; view them with [DJV](video-tools.md#djv-review-renders-and-image-sequences) or convert them: `oiiotool ~/mitsuba.exr -o ~/mitsuba.png`. Mitsuba 3 can render in RGB or **spectral** mode, and can compute how the picture changes when the scene changes (for research and machine learning). Documentation: <https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/>.

## appleseed

Only the command-line renderer is included (the *appleseed.studio* editor needs Python 2.7, which Debian 12 no longer has). The menu entry asks for a `.appleseed` project, renders it and shows the result.

```
appleseed.cli "/opt/animux/appleseed/examples/cpp/helloworld/reference output/test.appleseed" --output ~/appleseed.png
```

## pbrt-v4

The renderer from the free online book *Physically Based Rendering* (<https://pbr-book.org/>). The book explains every line of its source code.

```
cd /usr/share/animux/samples/pbrt
pbrt --spp 64 --outfile ~/pbrt.exr animux-spheres.pbrt
imgtool convert ~/pbrt.exr ~/pbrt.png
```

`--spp` sets the samples per pixel (quality). The Animux build runs on the processor only. Large example scenes: <https://github.com/mmp/pbrt-v4-scenes>.

## Gaffer + Cycles

[Gaffer](gaffer.md) can also render with Cycles from a node graph, the way lighting artists work in studios.

## Render times, roughly

| What | Typical time per frame on a 4-core PC |
|---|---|
| EEVEE, 1080p, simple scene | 1–10 seconds (with a graphics card) |
| Cycles CPU, 1080p, 128 samples with denoising | 30 seconds – 5 minutes |
| POV-Ray, 1280×720, sample scene | a few seconds |
| LuxCore / Mitsuba / pbrt, sample scenes | under a minute |

A 2-minute film at 24 frames per second has **2,880 frames**. Several minutes per frame quickly means days. Test with small resolution and few samples, and use a [render farm](flamenco.md) or render overnight.


---
<!-- page: software/renderer-comparison (md/software/renderer-comparison.md) -->
# Renderer comparison

> The seven renderers in Animux side by side: full name, who makes it, how it calculates light, what it runs on, what it does best and when to use it.

A renderer turns a 3D scene into a picture. They differ in **how they calculate light**: following rays of light like a camera does (*path tracing*), drawing the scene the way games do (*rasterisation*), or following light from both the camera and the lamps (*bidirectional*). That decides what each one is good at. Animux installs all seven, ready to use.

<div class="matrix" markdown="1">

| | Full name | Made by | How it calculates light | Runs on | Best at | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cycles** | Cycles Render Engine | Blender Foundation, in Blender | Path tracing, physically based | Processor or graphics card | Realistic light, soft shadows, glass, built-in denoising | Final frames of most films; also renders from Gaffer |
| **EEVEE** | Extra Easy Virtual Environment Engine | Blender Foundation, in Blender | Rasterisation (real time) with ray-traced reflections | Graphics card | Instant feedback, stylised and cartoon looks | Previews, motion graphics, stylised films (*Flow* was rendered in EEVEE) |
| **POV-Ray** | Persistence of Vision Raytracer | POV-Ray team, since 1991 | Ray tracing from a scene written as text | Processor | Exact shapes from maths, scenes as code | Teaching, maths art, generated scenes |
| **LuxCoreRender** | LuxCoreRender | LuxCoreRender project | Unbiased path tracing and bidirectional path tracing | Processor (GPU with a driver) | Caustics, light through glass and water, interiors | Product shots, architecture, the most accurate light |
| **appleseed** | appleseed | appleseed project | Physically based path tracing, OSL shaders | Processor | Production-style scenes and shading networks | Studying a VFX production renderer |
| **Mitsuba 3** | Mitsuba 3 | Realistic Graphics Lab, EPFL | Spectral and polarised path tracing; differentiable | Processor | Light by wavelength; works backwards from a picture to the scene | Research, scientific images, inverse rendering |
| **pbrt-v4** | Physically Based Rendering, version 4 | Pharr, Jakob and Humphreys | Spectral path tracing, explained line by line in a book | Processor | Every line of code explained in the book | Learning how renderers work |

</div>

## Which one, when?

| You want… | Take |
|---|---|
| A finished, realistic frame from Blender | **Cycles** |
| To see the light while you work, or a stylised look | **EEVEE** |
| One light rig for many shots, studio-style | **Gaffer** with Cycles ([Gaffer](gaffer.md)) |
| Caustics and glass that must be physically right | **LuxCoreRender** |
| To describe a scene in code | **POV-Ray** |
| To research or learn rendering | **Mitsuba 3**, **pbrt-v4** |

## Shaders: OSL

**OSL** (Open Shading Language) describes materials as small programs. It was developed at Sony Pictures Imageworks and is the shader language of film rendering: Cycles, appleseed and Gaffer read OSL, so one material works in all three. Animux includes the OSL compiler `oslc` ([Pipeline formats](pipeline-formats.md#osl-open-shading-language)).

How to start each renderer, sample scenes and render times: [Renderers](renderers.md).


---
<!-- page: software/flamenco (md/software/flamenco.md) -->
# Flamenco render farm

> Let several computers render one Blender animation together, using Flamenco Manager, Workers and shared storage, and the Animux render farm boot roles.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Flamenco | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 3D Animation → Render Queue Managers → Flamenco Manager |
| Version | 3.9.3 |
| Command | `animux-flamenco-manager` |
| Good for | Intermediate |
| Files | Blender jobs |
| Licence | GPL-3.0 |
| Website | [flamenco.blender.org](https://flamenco.blender.org/) |
| Self-test | `animux-selftest flamenco` |

</div>


A **render farm** is a group of computers that share the rendering of an animation: each computer renders different frames. **Flamenco** is Blender's official, free render farm software.

| Part | Runs on | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Manager** | one computer (it can also render) | keeps the list of jobs and hands out frames; has a web page to watch progress |
| **Worker** | every computer that renders | asks the Manager for work, runs Blender, reports back |
| **Blender add-on** | the artist's computer | sends a `.blend` file to the Manager as a job |
| **Shared storage** | a network folder | all computers must see the project files and write the frames, at the same path |

## 1. Shared storage

Every computer must reach the project at the same place, for example `/mnt/farm`. The simplest way on an all-Animux farm is NFS from the Manager computer.

On the Manager, first create the folder:

```
sudo mkdir -p /srv/farm
```

**Only if the Manager runs from the USB stick (live session):** the live system disk lives in memory, and NFS cannot share folders on it. Put the folder on a real disk or USB drive (mount it on `/srv/farm`), or, for a test, on a RAM disk of 8 GB:

```
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=8G tmpfs /srv/farm
```

(A RAM disk uses memory and is emptied when the Manager switches off, so copy the finished frames away.)

Then share it (change `192.168.1.0/24` to your own network):

```
sudo chown $USER /srv/farm
echo '/srv/farm 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,fsid=0)' | sudo tee -a /etc/exports
sudo systemctl unmask nfs-kernel-server && sudo systemctl enable --now nfs-kernel-server
sudo exportfs -ra && sudo exportfs -v
sudo ln -s /srv/farm /mnt/farm
```

`sudo exportfs -v` must list `/srv/farm`. `fsid=0` makes `/srv/farm` the top of the share, so the Workers mount `manager-pc:/` (this also works in a live session, where the plain path does not).

On each Worker (replace `manager-pc` with the Manager's name or IP address):

```
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/farm
sudo mount -t nfs manager-pc:/ /mnt/farm
```

A Windows share or NAS works too, as long as every computer uses the same path.

## 2. Start the Manager

On the Manager computer: **3D Animation → Render Queue Managers → Flamenco Manager**. A terminal window opens (keep it open; closing it stops the Manager) and the browser shows the setup page at `http://localhost:8080/`:

![Flamenco Manager's first-time setup in the browser.](../../images/flamenco.webp)

The setup asks for:

1. **Shared storage**: `/mnt/farm`.
2. **Blender**: choose *Blender found on $PATH* (`/usr/bin/blender`, Blender 5.2.3).

Settings and the job database are kept in `~/flamenco`. Without a desktop (text login), start the Manager with the same command the menu uses: `animux-flamenco-manager`, and open `http://manager-pc:8080/` from another computer.

!!! danger "Only Animux r16 (`_21`): Workers get no work"
    Fixed in r16.1 (`_25`). On r16 the Manager accepts jobs, but no Worker ever starts them: the Manager tries to keep its task logs in `/opt/animux/flamenco/flamenco-manager-storage`, where it may not write (the web page shows the tasks as *queued* forever). Fix it once, **after** the setup page, in a terminal on the Manager:

    ```
    sed -i "s#^local_manager_storage_path:.*#local_manager_storage_path: $HOME/flamenco/flamenco-manager-storage#" ~/flamenco/flamenco-manager.yaml
    ```

    then close the Manager window and start it again. The package `animux-flamenco` 3.9.3-animux2 does this by itself.

## 3. Start the Workers

On every render computer (including the Manager, if it should render too), open a terminal:

```
flamenco-worker
```

Workers find the Manager on the local network by themselves. If not, tell them where it is:

```
flamenco-worker -manager http://manager-pc:8080/
```

The Manager's web page lists them under **Workers**.

## 4. Send a job from Blender

1. On the artist's computer open `http://manager-pc:8080/` in Firefox and download the **Blender add-on** from the Manager's web page (the link on the start page).
2. In Blender: **Edit → Preferences → Add-ons → Install from Disk** (in the menu at the top right of the add-ons list) → choose the downloaded `flamenco-addon.zip`, and tick it. Enter the Manager URL and click **Check**.
3. Save your `.blend` file **inside the shared storage** (`/mnt/farm/my-short/sh010.blend`).
4. In **Properties → Output → Flamenco**, choose the job type **Simple Blender Render**, then **Submit to Flamenco**.

The frames appear in the shared storage as they are finished; watch progress on the web page.

## Animux render farm roles

The [boot menu](../start/boot-menu.md) has two farm entries for computers started from the ISO:

| Entry | What Animux does |
|---|---|
| **Render Farm Master** | unmasks the NFS and DHCP server services, so the steps above work |
| **Render Farm Slave** | a render node |

!!! warning "Known problems in r16 (`_21`), fixed in r16.1 (`_25`)"
    - Both entries still **start the desktop** (with automatic login); they were meant to start to a text login. This does no harm: open a terminal and follow the steps above.
    - Every computer started this way is called **animux**, so the Manager lists all Workers under the same name. Before starting `flamenco-worker` for the first time, give each computer its own name, for example `sudo hostnamectl set-hostname node1` (the Worker registers under the computer name).

    Both are fixed in r16.1 (`_25`, package `animux-roles` 1.0.19): text login and names like `animux-slave-3f2a`.

The DHCP server needs your own `/etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf` before it is useful, and **must not run on a network that already has a router handing out addresses**.

## Farmerjoe

**Farmerjoe** is the small render farm from the original Animux, kept for old projects (`/opt/farmerjoe`, its README opens from the menu). Use Flamenco for new work.

## Tips

- All computers should run the **same Blender version** (all Animux r16 computers do).
- Use **relative paths** and *File → External Data → Pack Resources* or keep textures in the shared storage.
- Render to **image sequences** (PNG or EXR), never directly to a video file: a crashed frame can be re-rendered, and every Worker writes its own frames.
- Wired network (1 Gbit/s or faster) is much better than Wi-Fi.
- Documentation: <https://flamenco.blender.org/usage/>.

## Coming: OpenCue

<div class="films">

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Sony Pictures Imageworks and Google Cloud · open source since January 2019</p>
<h2 class="film-title">OpenCue</h2>
<p class="made">Render manager for large studios · planned for Animux r17</p>
<p>OpenCue grew out of <b>Cue 3</b>, the queuing system Sony Pictures Imageworks developed in-house over 15 years and used on more than a hundred feature films and visual-effects projects. Google Cloud and Imageworks released it as open source (Apache 2.0) on 24 January 2019; it is now a project of the Academy Software Foundation.</p>
<p>Recent Imageworks projects ran it on over 150,000 processor cores, split between their own data centre and Google Cloud. Flamenco is the simpler choice for a class or a small studio; OpenCue is made for studios with many render nodes and many shows at once.</p>
<p class="source">Sources: Google Cloud blog, "Introducing OpenCue: an open source render manager for media and entertainment", 24 January 2019 · TechCrunch, "Google partners with Sony Pictures Imageworks to launch an open-source VFX render manager", 24 January 2019</p>
</article>

</div>


---
<!-- page: software/gaffer (md/software/gaffer.md) -->
# Gaffer

> The node-based lighting and look-development tool used by film studios, included with Cortex, OSL, OpenUSD and Alembic, and rendering with Cycles.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Gaffer | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 3D Animation → Pipeline Tools → Gaffer |
| Version | 1.7.5.0 |
| Command | `gaffer` |
| Good for | Advanced |
| Files | .gfr; reads USD, Alembic, SceneCache |
| Licence | BSD-3-Clause |
| Website | [gafferhq.org](https://www.gafferhq.org/) |
| Self-test | `animux-selftest gaffer` |

</div>


**Gaffer** is a free tool from Image Engine, a visual-effects studio, for the work *after* modelling and animation: **assembling scenes, lighting, look development (materials) and sending renders**. Everything is a **node graph**: boxes connected by lines, each doing one step. Change an early node and everything after it updates. This makes it possible to light hundreds of shots the same way.

!!! note "Is Gaffer for me?"
    For a personal or school film, **Blender alone is enough**. Gaffer is worth learning if you want to work in a VFX or animation studio pipeline, or your project has many shots that share lighting.

![Gaffer: the viewer at the top, the node graph at the bottom left, node settings on the right.](../../images/gaffer.webp)

## Start

**3D Animation → Pipeline Tools → Gaffer**, or `gaffer`. Gaffer's window has:

- **Viewer**: the 3D scene (or rendered image) produced by the selected node;
- **Graph Editor**: the nodes; press **Tab** in it to add a node by name;
- **Node Editor**: settings of the selected node;
- **Hierarchy / Scene Inspector**: the objects in the scene at that point of the graph.

## A first graph

Add nodes with **Tab** in the Graph Editor and connect an output (bottom of a node) to an input (top) by dragging. The sample scene uses this chain:

1. **Sphere**, **Plane**, **Camera** and two **CyclesLight** nodes (one `background_light` for the sky, one `distant_light` for the sun) → all into one **Group**.
2. **CyclesShader** (`principled_bsdf`, pick a base colour) + **PathFilter** (path `/group/sphere`) → **ShaderAssignment**: gives the sphere its material.
3. **StandardOptions**: switch on *Render Camera* (`/group/camera`) and *Resolution*.
4. **CyclesOptions**: samples and other Cycles settings.
5. **Outputs**: where the image is written (add an *Interactive* output for previews, a *Batch* output for files).
6. **InteractiveRender** (live preview in the Viewer) or **Render** (writes the files), renderer **Cycles**.

The sample `/usr/share/animux/samples/gaffer/render.py` builds such a graph by script and renders it:

```
gaffer env python /usr/share/animux/samples/gaffer/render.py ~/gaffer.exr
```

## Bringing in scenes

`SceneReader` nodes load **USD** (`.usd`, `.usda`, `.usdc`) and **Alembic** (`.abc`) files exported from Blender (**File → Export → Universal Scene Description** or **Alembic**). Lighting stays in Gaffer; when the animation changes, re-export and Gaffer picks it up.

## What comes with it

Gaffer on Animux includes the libraries studios use, with command-line tools you can run directly:

| Library | Tools | See |
|---|---|---|
| **Cortex** | Python libraries for VFX pipelines (`import IECore` inside `gaffer python`) | <https://github.com/ImageEngine/cortex> |
| **OpenUSD** | `usdview`, `usdcat`, `usdchecker`, `usdtree`, `usddiff`, `usdrecord`, `usdzip`, `usdresolve`, `usdedit`, `usdstitch` | [Pipeline formats](pipeline-formats.md#openusd) |
| **OSL** | `oslc`, `oslinfo`, `testshade` | [Pipeline formats](pipeline-formats.md#osl-open-shading-language) |
| **Alembic** | `abcls`, `abctree`, `abcecho`, `abcechobounds`, `abcconvert`, `abcstitcher` | [Pipeline formats](pipeline-formats.md#alembic) |
| **Cycles** | renders from Gaffer | |
| **OpenColorIO** | colour management | [Pipeline formats](pipeline-formats.md#opencolorio) |

## Command line and scripting

```
gaffer execute -script lighting.gfr -nodes CyclesRender -frames 1-100
gaffer python myscript.py
```

Learn more: <https://www.gafferhq.org/documentation/> and Gaffer's **Help** menu (examples and tutorials are built in).

<!-- page: software/pipeline-formats (md/software/pipeline-formats.md) -->
# Pipeline formats and tools

> OpenUSD, Alembic, OpenEXR, OpenColorIO, OpenVDB, OSL and MaterialX, what each studio format is for and the tools Animux has for it.

Studios pass work between many programs. These open formats, most of them from the *Academy Software Foundation*, make that possible. Blender reads and writes most of them; Animux adds the command-line tools to check and convert them. Who made each format and why, in one card each: [Studio formats](studio-formats.md).

| Format | Holds | File | Blender |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenUSD** | whole scenes: objects, materials, lights, cameras, layers | `.usd .usda .usdc .usdz` | File → Import/Export → USD |
| **Alembic** | baked moving geometry (animation caches) | `.abc` | File → Import/Export → Alembic |
| **OpenEXR** | high-quality images, many layers (passes) | `.exr` | Output file format OpenEXR |
| **OpenColorIO** | colour spaces and looks | `config.ocio` | Blender uses OCIO internally |
| **OpenVDB** | volumes: smoke, fire, clouds | `.vdb` | Add → Volume → Import OpenVDB |
| **OSL** | custom materials as code | `.osl` | Cycles → Script node (CPU) |
| **MaterialX** | materials shared between programs | `.mtlx` | via USD export |

## OpenUSD

Universal Scene Description, made by Pixar, is the scene format of modern pipelines (Blender, Houdini, Maya, Omniverse, Unreal).

```
usdview /usr/share/animux/samples/usd/animux-scene.usda   # look at a scene
usdcat scene.usda -o scene.usdc                          # text → binary
usdcat scene.usdc                                        # print a binary file as text
usdtree scene.usda                                       # list what is inside
usdchecker scene.usda                                    # check for errors
usdzip -a scene.usdz scene.usda                          # package for AR (iPhone)
```

![usdview showing the Animux sample scene.](../../images/usdview.webp)

Python: `animux-vfx-python -c "from pxr import Usd; print(Usd.Stage.Open('scene.usda').GetRootLayer().ExportToString())"`.

## Alembic

```
abcls -r /usr/share/animux/samples/alembic/animux-cube.abc   # list objects
abctree file.abc                                           # show the hierarchy
abcecho file.abc                                           # print details
```

The sample is a cube spinning over 24 frames. Import it in Blender with **File → Import → Alembic**.

## OpenEXR and OpenImageIO

EXR keeps real light values (brighter than white) and several **passes** in one file: diffuse, specular, depth, object IDs. Render to EXR, then grade and comp.

```
exrheader render.exr                       # what is inside (channels, compression)
oiiotool render.exr -o render.png          # convert
oiiotool render.exr --resize 50% -o half.exr
oiiotool a.exr b.exr --over -o comp.exr    # put a over b
iinfo -v render.exr
```

View EXR files with [DJV](video-tools.md#djv-review-renders-and-image-sequences).

## OpenColorIO

OCIO describes colour spaces (sRGB, ACEScg, Filmic/AgX…) so every program shows the same colours.

```
ociocheck --iconfig /usr/share/animux/samples/ocio/config.ocio
```

Point programs to a config with the `OCIO` environment variable: `OCIO=/path/config.ocio krita`.

## OpenVDB

```
vdb_print -l smoke.vdb
```

Blender writes VDB files from smoke simulations (*Physics → Fluid → Cache → Format: OpenVDB*).

## OSL (Open Shading Language)

```
oslc stripes.osl          # compile to stripes.oso
oslinfo stripes.oso       # list its parameters
```

In Blender: Cycles, **Device: CPU**, tick **Open Shading Language** in Render properties, then add a **Script** node in the shader editor.

## Animux VFX Python

`animux-vfx-python` is a Python 3.11 with all these libraries installed together, so scripts work without setup:

| Module | Import as |
|---|---|
| OpenUSD (usd-core 26.11) | `from pxr import Usd, UsdGeom` |
| OpenImageIO 3.2 | `import OpenImageIO as oiio` |
| OpenEXR 3.5 | `import OpenEXR` |
| OpenColorIO 2.6 | `import PyOpenColorIO as ocio` |
| MaterialX 1.39 | `import MaterialX` |
| Mitsuba 3.9 | `import mitsuba as mi` |
| LuxCoreRender 2.11 | `import pyluxcore` |
| NumPy 2.4 | `import numpy` |

It lives in `/opt/animux/vfx-env` and is managed by the `animux-vfx-python` package; do not install into it. For extra libraries make your own environment on top of it: `/opt/animux/vfx-env/bin/python -m venv --system-site-packages ~/myenv`, then `~/myenv/bin/pip install name`.

<!-- page: software/studio-formats (md/software/studio-formats.md) -->
# Studio formats

> OpenUSD, Alembic, OpenEXR, OpenColorIO and OpenVDB, one card each: which studio made it, what problem it solves, and what it looks like in Animux.

A film passes through many programs: modelling, animation, effects, lighting, compositing. Each step must read what the step before wrote, without losing anything. The big studios solved this with their own file formats and then **gave them away as open source**. Today most of them are kept by the **Academy Software Foundation** (ASWF), part of the Linux Foundation. Animux installs them with their tools.

<div class="films">

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Pixar · open source since 2016</p>
<h2 class="film-title">OpenUSD</h2>
<p class="made">Universal Scene Description · <code>.usd .usda .usdc</code> · viewer: <code>usdview</code></p>
<p><b>The problem:</b> on one shot, modelling, layout, animation and lighting all want to work at the same time.</p>
<p><b>The answer:</b> a scene made of <b>layers</b>. Each department writes its own layer on top of the others, and a stronger layer wins. Nobody overwrites anybody's file.</p>
<p>Pixar built USD for its own films and released it in 2016. It is now read by Blender, Houdini, Maya, Unreal and NVIDIA Omniverse.</p>
<p class="source">Source: Pixar, "Open Source Announcement", openusd.org</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Sony Pictures Imageworks and ILM · 2010</p>
<h2 class="film-title">Alembic</h2>
<p class="made">Baked animation cache · <code>.abc</code> · tools: <code>abcls</code>, <code>abctree</code></p>
<p><b>The problem:</b> a rig only works in the program it was built in.</p>
<p><b>The answer:</b> the finished movement is <b>baked</b>: every vertex position on every frame is stored. The cache plays the same in Blender, Gaffer, Houdini or Maya, with no rig needed.</p>
<p>Imageworks and Industrial Light &amp; Magic announced it together at SIGGRAPH 2010.</p>
<p class="source">Source: Alembic project, alembic.io</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Industrial Light &amp; Magic · open source since 2003</p>
<h2 class="film-title">OpenEXR</h2>
<p class="made">High dynamic range images · <code>.exr</code> · viewer: <a class="chip" href="video-tools.md">DJV</a></p>
<p><b>The problem:</b> a PNG cuts off light: the sun and a lamp both become plain white.</p>
<p><b>The answer:</b> EXR keeps the <b>real brightness</b> of every pixel, so exposure can be changed later, and stores <b>passes</b> (light, shadow, reflections, depth) as separate layers in one file for compositing.</p>
<p class="source">Source: OpenEXR project, openexr.com</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">Sony Pictures Imageworks</p>
<h2 class="film-title">OpenColorIO</h2>
<p class="made">Colour management · <code>config.ocio</code> · ACES</p>
<p><b>The problem:</b> the same frame looks different in the 3D program, the compositor and the editor.</p>
<p><b>The answer:</b> one <b>colour configuration</b> shared by every program, so a red stays the same red from render to final grade. Blender, Krita, Gaffer and DaVinci Resolve all use it.</p>
<p class="source">Source: OpenColorIO project, opencolorio.org</p>
</article>

<article class="film">
<p class="kicker">DreamWorks Animation · 2012</p>
<h2 class="film-title">OpenVDB</h2>
<p class="made">Volumes · <code>.vdb</code> · smoke, fire, clouds</p>
<p><b>The problem:</b> smoke and clouds are mostly empty air, and storing every point of a box wastes memory.</p>
<p><b>The answer:</b> a sparse grid that stores only the cells where something is. Blender writes its smoke simulations as VDB, and renderers read them.</p>
<p class="source">Source: OpenVDB project, openvdb.org</p>
</article>

</div>

Commands and examples for each format: [Pipeline formats](pipeline-formats.md).


---
<!-- page: software/synfig (md/software/synfig.md) -->
# Synfig Studio

> 2D vector animation with automatic in-between frames and bone rigs. Ideal for cut-out characters, motion graphics and explainer films.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Synfig Studio | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 2D Animation → Synfig Studio |
| Version | 1.5.1 |
| Command | `synfigstudio` |
| Good for | Beginner |
| Files | .sifz, .sif; exports PNG sequences, GIF, video |
| Licence | GPL-3.0 |
| Website | [synfig.org](https://www.synfig.org/) |
| Self-test | `animux-selftest synfig` |

</div>


In **Synfig** you do not draw every frame. You set the important poses (**waypoints**) and Synfig calculates the frames in between (**tweening**). Characters are built from shapes and can be moved with **bones**, like a puppet.

![Synfig Studio with the Animux bouncing-ball sample: canvas in the middle, tools on the left, parameters and layers on the right, timetrack at the bottom.](../../images/synfig.webp)

## The window

| Panel | Use |
|---|---|
| **Toolbox** (left) | transform, circle, rectangle, spline (draw shapes), fill, text, bones… |
| **Canvas** (middle) | your picture; the **Animation mode** button at its bottom right (red when on) records changes as waypoints |
| **Params** | settings of the selected layer (colour, position, radius…) |
| **Layers** | every shape is a layer; group them to build characters |
| **Timetrack** | waypoints over time; drag them to change timing |

## Animate a ball in five steps

The sample `/usr/share/animux/samples/synfig/bouncing-ball.sif` is a finished example; open it with **File → Open** to look at it. To make your own:

1. **File → New**. Set the length in **Canvas → Properties → Time** (for example *End time* 48 at 24 fps = 2 seconds).
2. Choose the **Circle tool** and drag on the canvas to draw a ball.
3. Click the **Animation mode** button (bottom right of the canvas): the canvas gets a red frame.
4. At frame 0, place the ball at the top. Move the time slider to frame 12 and drag the ball to the bottom; at frame 24 back to the top. Synfig adds waypoints and fills in the frames.
5. Press **Play**. Turn animation mode off when you are done.

Make it look natural: right-click a waypoint → **Both → Ease In/Out** for slow-in and slow-out.

## Export

**File → Render**: choose the file name and **Target**:

- `png` (image sequence, best quality, for editing in Kdenlive),
- `gif` for the web,
- `ffmpeg` for a video file.

Or from a terminal:

```
synfig bouncing-ball.sif -t png -o ~/ball/frame.png        # all frames
synfig bouncing-ball.sif -t gif -o ~/ball.gif
synfig bouncing-ball.sif -t png --time 12 -o ~/frame12.png  # one frame
```

## Learn more

- Synfig's manual and tutorials: <https://synfig.readthedocs.io/>
- Tutorial on this guide: [A bouncing ball in Synfig](../tutorials/bouncing-ball-synfig.md)


---
<!-- page: software/opentoonz (md/software/opentoonz.md) -->
# OpenToonz

> The studio 2D animation program: hand-drawn and cut-out animation with the Xsheet, scan cleanup, ink and paint, and node-based effects. New in r16.3.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| OpenToonz | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 2D Animation → OpenToonz |
| Version | 1.8.0 (built by Animux, new in r16.3) |
| Command | `opentoonz` |
| Good for | Intermediate |
| Files | .tnz scenes with .tlv, .pli and raster levels; renders PNG/TIFF sequences and video |
| Licence | BSD-3-Clause |
| Website | [opentoonz.github.io](https://opentoonz.github.io/) |
| Self-test | `animux-selftest opentoonz` |

</div>


**OpenToonz** is the open-source version of **Toonz**, the 2D animation software used in studios, among them Studio Ghibli, whose edition it is based on. It covers the whole traditional 2D pipeline: draw or scan the drawings, clean up the lines, paint them, time them on the **Xsheet**, add effects and render.

!!! note "New in r16.3"
    OpenToonz is on Animux from release **r16.3**. Debian has no OpenToonz package, so Animux builds version 1.8.0 from its source code (package `animux-opentoonz`, installed in `/opt/animux/opentoonz`).

## Start it

**2D Animation → OpenToonz**, or type `opentoonz`. The first start copies OpenToonz's brushes, templates and settings to `~/.config/OpenToonz`; that takes a few seconds.

The **Startup** window opens on top:

1. Keep the project **sandbox** (OpenToonz's practice project), or click **New Project...** for a real one.
2. Click **Create a New Scene**, type a **Scene Name** and click **Create Scene**.

Untick **Show this at startup** if you do not want this window every time.

## The main parts

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Rooms** (tabs top right) | ready-made window layouts: *Drawing*, *Timeline*, *Cleanup*, *InknPaint*, *Xsheet*, … |
| **Viewer** | the canvas; the red frame is the camera |
| **Xsheet** / **Timeline** | columns are layers, rows are frames: which drawing is shown on which frame |
| **Level Strip** | all drawings of the current level |
| **FX Schematic** | effects as connected nodes (*Windows → Schematic*) |

A **level** is a set of drawings (one character, one prop). OpenToonz has three kinds: **Toonz Raster** (`.tlv`, pencil-like lines with separate ink and paint), **Toonz Vector** (`.pli`, editable lines) and plain **Raster** (`.tif`, `.png`).

## A first drawing

1. In the **Drawing** room, click the cell of frame 1 in column *Col1*.
2. Press **B** for the **Brush** and draw in the viewer. OpenToonz makes a new level for it.
3. Click frame 2 and draw the next pose. **Onion skin** (*View → Onion Skin*) shows the frame before.
4. **File → Save All** (**Ctrl+S**). The scene goes to `scenes/`, the drawings to `drawings/` of the project.
5. **Render → Output Settings** to choose the format and folder, then **Render → Render** (**Ctrl+Shift+R**). Files go to the project's `outputs/` folder.

A ready-made sample project is in `/usr/share/animux/samples/opentoonz/animux-lines`; `animux-selftest opentoonz` renders it.

## Render without the window

OpenToonz renders with **tcomposer**. After you have started OpenToonz once:

```
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/animux/opentoonz/lib/opentoonz \
  /opt/animux/opentoonz/bin/tcomposer ~/.config/OpenToonz/stuff/sandbox/scenes/myscene.tnz -o /tmp/out.png
```

This writes `/tmp/out.0001.png`, `/tmp/out.0002.png`, … one file per frame. On a server without a screen, put `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen` in front.

## When to use something else

- Simple frame-by-frame drawing, for beginners and schools: [Pencil2D](pencil2d.md).
- Animation by moving shapes and bones with automatic in-betweens: [Synfig](synfig.md).
- Painterly animation with brushes and textures: [Krita](krita.md).

Help: the OpenToonz manual at [opentoonz.readthedocs.io](https://opentoonz.readthedocs.io/).


---
<!-- page: software/pencil2d (md/software/pencil2d.md) -->
# Pencil2D and TupiTube

> Hand-drawn, frame-by-frame animation the traditional way, with onion skin, a timeline and export to video or GIF.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Pencil2D | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 2D Animation → Pencil2D |
| Version | 0.6.6 |
| Command | `pencil2d` |
| Good for | Beginner |
| Files | .pclx; exports PNG sequence, GIF, MP4 |
| Licence | GPL-2.0 |
| Website | [pencil2d.org](https://www.pencil2d.org/) |

</div>


**Pencil2D** works like a flip book: you draw a picture on each frame and play them in a row. **Onion skin** shows the previous and next drawings faintly, so you can draw the in-betweens. It is simple enough for children and good enough for professional rough animation.

![Pencil2D: tools on the left, the canvas in the middle, colours on the right, the timeline with layers at the bottom.](../../images/pencil2d.webp)

## Layer types

| Layer | For |
|---|---|
| **Bitmap** | pencil and brush drawing, like paper |
| **Vector** | clean lines you can still edit; fill areas with the bucket |
| **Camera** | pan and zoom over the drawing |
| **Sound** | dialogue or music to time your animation |

## A first animation

See the full tutorial: **[Hand-drawn animation in Pencil2D](../tutorials/hand-drawn-pencil2d.md)**. In short:

1. Draw on frame 1.
2. Click frame 3 in the timeline and click **+** (*Add Frame*); draw the next pose.
3. Switch on **onion skin** (the onion buttons above the timeline) to see the frame before.
4. Press **Play**. Change the speed with the **FPS** box (12 fps is common for hand-drawn animation, "on twos" at 24 fps).
5. **File → Export → Movie** for MP4 or GIF, or **Image Sequence** for PNG files.

Pencil2D saves projects as `.pclx`.

## TupiTube

**TupiTube** (Debian package `tupi`) is another beginner-friendly 2D animation program, made for schools: draw, tween objects between positions, and export. Start it from **2D Animation → TupiTube** or `tupi`.

![TupiTube.](../../images/tupitube.webp)

## When to use something else

- Painting-style animation with brushes and textures: [Krita](krita.md).
- Animation by moving shapes and bones instead of drawing every frame: [Synfig](synfig.md).
- 2D drawing combined with 3D: Grease Pencil in [Blender](blender.md#grease-pencil-2d-inside-blender).


---
<!-- page: software/krita (md/software/krita.md) -->
# Krita

> Professional digital painting with hundreds of brushes, layers, a drawing-tablet-friendly interface and a full frame-by-frame animation timeline.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Krita | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 2D Graphics → Bitmap Editors → Krita |
| Version | 5.3.4.1 |
| Command | `krita` |
| Good for | Beginner to professional |
| Files | .kra; PSD, PNG, JPEG, EXR, TIFF; renders animation to video |
| Licence | GPL-3.0 |
| Website | [krita.org](https://krita.org/) |

</div>


Krita is made by artists for **painting**: concept art, character design, backgrounds, textures, comics and storyboards. It also has a complete **animation** workspace for hand-drawn animation with brushes.

![Krita's welcome screen. Start a new file on the left; recent files are in the middle.](../../images/krita.webp)

## Start painting

1. **File → New** → choose a size (for film: *1920 × 1080*, 300 dpi for print) → **Create**.
2. Pick a brush in **Brush Presets** (right), a colour in the **Advanced Color Selector**.
3. Paint. **[ ]** change brush size, **E** switches to eraser mode, **Ctrl+Z** undoes.
4. Add layers with **Insert**, or the **+** in the Layers panel. Keep sketch, line art and colour on separate layers.
5. **File → Save** as `.kra` (keeps layers); **File → Export** to PNG or JPEG.

## Animation

1. **Window → Workspace → Animation**. The **Timeline** and **Animation** panels appear.
2. Draw on frame 0. In the timeline, click the next frame, right-click → **Create Blank Frame**, and draw.
3. **Onion Skins** panel: see the frames before and after.
4. Set the frame rate and start/end in the **Animation** panel; press **Play**.
5. **File → Render Animation**: choose **Video** (MP4, uses FFmpeg) or **Image Sequence**.

## Drawing tablets

Pressure works out of the box. Tune it in **Settings → Configure Krita → Tablet settings** (pressure curve). If the cursor is offset on a multi-monitor setup, set the tablet's area in Krita's tablet settings.

## Colour management

**Settings → Configure Krita → Color Management** selects the screen profile and OCIO configuration; important when you paint textures or matte paintings for 3D.

## Learn more

- Krita manual: <https://docs.krita.org/>
- Tutorial on this guide: [Paint an animation in Krita](../tutorials/krita-animation.md)

<!-- page: software/stopmotion (md/software/stopmotion.md) -->
# Stopmotion

> Capture stop-motion animation with a webcam or import photos from a camera, check each pose with onion skin, and export a film.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Stopmotion (Linux Stopmotion) | |
|---|---|
| Menu | StopMotion Animation → Stopmotion |
| Version | 0.8.6 |
| Command | `stopmotion` |
| Good for | Beginner |
| Files | .dat project; image folders; exports video |
| Licence | GPL-2.0 |
| Website | [linuxstopmotion.org](http://linuxstopmotion.org/) |

</div>


Stop motion is animation with real objects: clay figures, LEGO, paper cut-outs, toys. You move the object a tiny bit, take a photo, move it again, take another. **Stopmotion** helps you take the photos and line up each new pose with the previous one.

![Stopmotion: the frame list on the left, the camera view in the middle.](../../images/stopmotion.webp)

## What you need

- A **webcam** (any USB webcam that works on Linux), or a camera whose photos you copy in afterwards.
- A **tripod** or something that holds the camera completely still.
- **Steady light**: close the curtains and use lamps. Daylight changes and makes the film flicker.

## Capturing with a webcam

1. Plug in the webcam and start **StopMotion Animation → Stopmotion**.
2. **Settings → Preferences → Video Import**: choose the device (`/dev/video0` is usually the first webcam).
3. Click the **camera button** to start the live view.
4. Turn on **onion skinning** (mix slider: 1 or 2 previous frames). The last photo shows faintly over the live image.
5. Move your figure a little, then press **Space** (or the capture button) to take a frame. Repeat.
6. Press **Play** to check the movement.

Twelve frames per second is a good start; 24 is smoother but needs twice as many photos.

## Photos from a camera

**Edit → Add frames** (or drag image files into the frame list) to add photos taken with a camera or phone. Rename them in order first (for example `0001.jpg`, `0002.jpg`).

## Sound and export

- Add sound with the **Sound** button of a scene.
- **File → Export → Video** writes a video file (it uses FFmpeg); **File → Export → Cinelerra** sends the frames to Cinelerra.
- Or export the frames and put them together with FFmpeg:
  ```
  ffmpeg -framerate 12 -i %04d.jpg -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 film.mp4
  ```

## In a virtual machine

The VM must pass the webcam through: in VirtualBox install the *Extension Pack* and use **Devices → Webcams**. See [VirtualBox](../start/virtualbox.md#webcam-for-stop-motion).

Tutorial: [Stop motion with a webcam](../tutorials/stop-motion-webcam.md).


---
<!-- page: software/gimp-inkscape (md/software/gimp-inkscape.md) -->
# GIMP, Inkscape and other image tools

> Photo editing with GIMP, vector drawing with Inkscape, sketching with MyPaint, pixel art with GrafX2 and mtPaint, and batch work with ImageMagick.

| Program | Best for | Start |
|---|---|---|
| **GIMP** 3.2 | fixing and retouching renders and photos, textures, cut-outs, batch editing | `gimp` |
| **Inkscape** 1.4 | logos, titles, clean character designs, backgrounds: shapes that stay sharp at any size (SVG) | `inkscape` |
| **MyPaint** 2.0 | fast sketching and concept painting on an endless canvas | `mypaint` |
| **GrafX2** 2.8 | pixel art and sprites with palettes | `grafx2` |
| **mtPaint** 3.40 | very quick pixel edits | `mtpaint` |
| **ImageMagick** | changing hundreds of images at once from the terminal | `convert`, `mogrify` |

## GIMP

![GIMP with the render from the first tutorial.](../../images/gimp.webp)

Common jobs:

- **Adjust a render**: *Colors → Curves* or *Levels*; *Colors → Hue-Saturation*.
- **Cut out a background**: *Tools → Selection Tools → Foreground Select*, then *Layer → Transparency → Add Alpha Channel* and delete.
- **Make a texture tile seamlessly**: *Filters → Map → Tile Seamless*.
- **Resize**: *Image → Scale Image*. **Export**: *File → Export As* (GIMP's own format is `.xcf`; *Export* writes PNG/JPEG).
- **Non-destructive filters** (new in GIMP 3): filters stay editable on the layer; click the **fx** icon in the Layers panel to change or remove them.
- **G'MIC** (hundreds of extra effects: painterly looks, denoise, cartoon) is not available for GIMP 3.2 on Animux yet. The previous GIMP 2.10 with G'MIC is still installed: type `gimp.debian` in a terminal and use *Filters → G'MIC-Qt* there.

!!! note "GIMP 3.2, Krita 5.3 and Inkscape 1.4"
    Animux r16.1 (`_25`) includes them; Debian's Krita 5.1 and Inkscape 1.2 are no longer on the ISO, and GIMP 2.10 stays as `gimp.debian` for G'MIC. Animux r16 (`_21`) shipped only GIMP 2.10, Krita 5.1 and Inkscape 1.2 from Debian 12; there, the packages `animux-gimp`, `animux-krita` and `animux-inkscape` add the official current versions (the menu entries and the commands `gimp`, `krita` and `inkscape` then start the new versions). Install them like a [guide update](../about/guide-updates.md#how-to-get-a-newer-guide) (package files or, once online, `sudo apt install animux-gimp animux-krita animux-inkscape`).

!!! tip "AI assistants in GIMP, Krita and Inkscape"
    An AI assistant can work in the new GIMP, Krita and Inkscape through MCP: `animux-mcp gimp on`, `animux-mcp krita on`, `animux-mcp inkscape on`. See [AI agents](ai-agents.md#1b-switch-on-gimp-krita-or-inkscape).

## Inkscape

![Inkscape.](../../images/inkscape.webp)

- Draw with the **rectangle, ellipse, star** and **Bézier pen** tools; colour with *Object → Fill and Stroke* (Ctrl+Shift+F).
- Text for titles: **T** tool; convert to shapes with *Path → Object to Path* before sharing the file.
- **Export** PNG at any size: *File → Export* (Ctrl+Shift+E). Inkscape files (SVG) also open in Blender (*File → Import → SVG*) and Synfig.

From the terminal: `inkscape title.svg --export-type=png --export-width=1920`.

GIMP also works without a window, for scripts and AI agents, with Python (GIMP 3 API):

```
gimp-console -i --batch-interpreter=python-fu-eval -b "exec(open('my_script.py').read())" --quit
```

## MyPaint

![MyPaint.](../../images/mypaint.webp)

Press **Tab** to hide the panels and paint full screen. The canvas grows as you paint. Save as `.ora` (OpenRaster, opens in Krita and GIMP).

## ImageMagick: many images at once

```
mogrify -resize 50% *.png                         # make every PNG half size (overwrites!)
mogrify -format jpg *.png                         # convert all PNG to JPEG
convert in.png -gravity south -pointsize 48 -annotate +0+20 "Shot 10" out.png
montage frame_*.png -tile 6x -geometry 320x180+4+4 contact-sheet.png
```

Work on a **copy** of your files: `mogrify` changes them in place.
