<!-- page: software/kdenlive (md/software/kdenlive.md) -->
# Kdenlive

> The recommended video editor on Animux. Put shots and sound on a timeline, add titles and transitions, and export an MP4 for YouTube or a festival.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Kdenlive | |
|---|---|
| Menu | NLV Editors → Kdenlive |
| Version | 22.12.3 |
| Command | `kdenlive` |
| Good for | Beginner |
| Files | .kdenlive projects; almost every video, audio and image format |
| Licence | GPL-3.0 |
| Website | [kdenlive.org](https://kdenlive.org/) |

</div>


When your shots are rendered, a **video editor** puts them together with dialogue, music and titles. **Kdenlive** is powerful and still easy to start with.

![Kdenlive with the turntable animation in the project bin and on the timeline.](../../images/kdenlive.webp)

## The window

| Area | Use |
|---|---|
| **Project Bin** (top left) | all your clips: videos, image sequences, sound, titles |
| **Clip Monitor / Project Monitor** (top right) | play the selected clip / the whole edit |
| **Effects, Transitions** (tabs) | drag them onto clips |
| **Timeline** (bottom) | video tracks (V1, V2…) and audio tracks (A1, A2…) |

## Edit a film in six steps

1. **Project → Project Settings**: choose the format of your film, for example *HD 1080p 24 fps*. Do this first.
2. **Add clips**: right-click in the Project Bin → **Add Clip or Folder** (or drag files from the file manager). For a numbered **image sequence** (`0001.png`, `0002.png`…), tick **Import image sequence** in the file dialog.
3. **Drag clips to the timeline** in order. Trim a clip by dragging its ends; cut at the playhead with **Shift+R**.
4. **Sound**: drag music and dialogue onto the audio tracks. Change volume with the *Volume* effect or the clip's line.
5. **Titles**: right-click the Bin → **Add Title Clip**. **Transitions**: overlap two clips on different tracks and add a *Dissolve* (*Wipe*, …).
6. **Export**: **Project → Render** (Ctrl+Enter) → preset **MP4-H264/AAC** → choose the file name → **Render to File**.

!!! tip "Big projects run slowly?"
    Turn on **proxy clips** (*Project Settings → Proxy*). Kdenlive edits small copies and uses the originals only for the final render.

## Good export settings

| For | Settings |
|---|---|
| YouTube / Vimeo | MP4-H264/AAC, same resolution and frame rate as the project, quality 18–23 |
| Festival / archive | ProRes or DNxHR (in the render presets) or a PNG image sequence + WAV |
| Phone / messaging | MP4-H264, 1280×720 |

Kdenlive also renders from the command line using the `melt` program it is built on.

Learn more: <https://docs.kdenlive.org/> · Tutorial: [Edit your film in Kdenlive](../tutorials/edit-video-kdenlive.md).


---
<!-- page: software/video-tools (md/software/video-tools.md) -->
# More video tools

> OpenShot, Cinelerra-GG and Avidemux for editing, HandBrake and FFmpeg for converting, DJV for reviewing renders, VLC for playing, and screen recording.

| Program | Use it to | Start |
|---|---|---|
| [Kdenlive](kdenlive.md) | edit a film (recommended) | `kdenlive` |
| **OpenShot** 2.6 | edit very simply: drag, drop, export | `openshot-qt` |
| **Cinelerra-GG** | edit with professional colour grading, compositing, motion tracking | `cin` |
| **Avidemux** 2.8 | cut a single file quickly, filter, re-encode | `avidemux` |
| **HandBrake** 1.6 | convert a finished film with ready presets | `ghb` |
| **FFmpeg** 5.1 | convert anything from the terminal; image sequence → video | `ffmpeg` |
| **DJV** 3.7 | play image sequences and EXR renders at true speed, compare versions | `djv` |
| **VLC** 3.0 | play every video and sound file | `vlc` |
| **MKVToolNix** | combine video, audio tracks and subtitles in one MKV | `mkvtoolnix-gui` |
| **Subtitle Editor**, **Gnome Subtitles** | write and time subtitles | `subtitleeditor` |

## OpenShot

![OpenShot.](../../images/openshot.webp)

Import files (Ctrl+F), drag them to a track, press **Export Video** (the red button). Good for school projects.

## Cinelerra-GG

![Cinelerra-GG has several windows: program, viewer, compositor and resources.](../../images/cinelerra.webp)

Cinelerra is very capable but different from other editors (several windows, many options). The manual is at <https://www.cinelerra-gg.org/download/CinelerraGG_Manual.pdf>.

## Avidemux

![Avidemux with the turntable video.](../../images/avidemux.webp)

Open a video, set **A** and **B** markers to select a part, choose *Video Output* (for example *Mpeg4 AVC (x264)*) or **Copy** to keep quality, and **File → Save**. Copy mode cuts without re-encoding, in seconds.

## HandBrake

![HandBrake.](../../images/handbrake.webp)

**Open Source** → choose your film → pick a **Preset** (for example *General → Fast 1080p30*) → **Start Encode**.

## DJV: review renders and image sequences

![DJV showing a render.](../../images/djv.webp)

Studios check renders with a player like DJV: it plays **image sequences** (`render_0001.exr` …) at the correct frame rate, shows EXR channels and exposure, and compares two versions side by side (*Compare* menu). **File → Open** and choose the first frame; DJV finds the rest of the sequence.

## FFmpeg: the five most useful commands

```
# PNG image sequence → MP4 video (24 frames per second)
ffmpeg -framerate 24 -i render_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 film.mp4

# add a soundtrack (stops at the shorter of the two)
ffmpeg -i film.mp4 -i music.wav -c:v copy -c:a aac -shortest film-with-sound.mp4

# make a GIF for the web (480 px wide)
ffmpeg -i film.mp4 -vf "fps=12,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos" film.gif

# cut 10 seconds starting at 0:05, without re-encoding
ffmpeg -ss 5 -i film.mp4 -t 10 -c copy clip.mp4

# record the screen (stop with q)
ffmpeg -f x11grab -framerate 30 -i :0.0 -c:v libx264 -preset ultrafast screen.mp4
```

`%04d` means "four-digit frame number": `render_0001.png`, `render_0002.png`… Change it to match your files.

## Screenshots and screen recording

- **Print** key: screenshot of the whole screen; **Alt+Print**: the window (*Screen Casting → Screenshot* for options).
- Record the screen with the FFmpeg command above. **OBS Studio** and **SimpleScreenRecorder** are not on the ISO in r16; install them with `sudo apt install obs-studio` or `simplescreenrecorder` (see [Adding software](../desktop/add-software.md)).


---
<!-- page: software/audio (md/software/audio.md) -->
# Sound and music

> Record voices with Audacity, mix the soundtrack in Ardour, compose with LMMS, Hydrogen and MuseScore, and understand how audio works on Animux.

| Program | Use it to | Start |
|---|---|---|
| **Audacity** 3.2 | record and clean up dialogue and sound effects (easiest) | `audacity` |
| **Ardour** 7.3 | record and mix many tracks, the full soundtrack of a film, with effects and automation | `ardour` |
| **LMMS** 1.2 | compose music with built-in synthesizers, beats and samples | `lmms` |
| **Hydrogen** 1.2 | program drum rhythms | `hydrogen` |
| **MuseScore 3** | write sheet music and play it back | `mscore3` |
| **Rosegarden** | MIDI sequencing and scoring | `rosegarden` |
| **ZynAddSubFX, Yoshimi, Qsynth, Guitarix, VMPK** | software instruments, guitar amp, on-screen keyboard | menu |
| **Sonic Visualiser, Praat** | look at sound; Praat analyses speech (useful for lip sync timing) | menu |
| **SoundConverter, SoX** | convert sound files | `soundconverter`, `sox` |

All are in **Sound Engineering**.

## Audacity: record a voice-over

![Audacity. The first time it shows a welcome window with links to help; click OK.](../../images/audacity.webp)

1. Plug in a microphone (a USB microphone or headset is easiest). Choose it in the **microphone** list on the toolbar.
2. Click the red **Record** button, speak, click **Stop**.
3. Clean it: select a quiet part → **Effect → Noise Removal and Repair → Noise Reduction → Get Noise Profile**; select everything (Ctrl+A) → Noise Reduction → **OK**. Then **Effect → Volume and Compression → Normalize**.
4. **File → Export → Export as WAV** (best for editing) or MP3.

## Ardour: mix the soundtrack

![The first time, Ardour runs a short setup assistant: click Forward through it (the defaults are fine).](../../images/ardour-first.webp)

When Ardour starts it asks for a **session** (project) and the **audio system**: choose **JACK/PipeWire** or **ALSA** (see below). Add tracks with **Track → Add Track, Bus or VCA**, import the dialogue, music and effects with **Session → Import**, and set levels in the **Mixer** window (Alt+M). **Session → Export → Export to Audio File(s)** writes the final mix.

To line up sound with picture inside Ardour, **Session → Open Video** needs the extra programs *harvid* and *xjadeo*, which are not included. The easier way: edit the final mix against the picture in [Kdenlive](kdenlive.md).

## LMMS and Hydrogen: make music

![The first time, LMMS asks to create its working folder in Documents: click Yes.](../../images/lmms-first.webp)

In **LMMS**, drag an instrument (for example *TripleOscillator*) from the left into the **Song Editor**, double-click its pattern to open the **Piano Roll** and draw notes. The **Beat+Bassline Editor** is for drum patterns. **File → Export** writes WAV or OGG.

In **Hydrogen**, click squares in the pattern grid to place drum hits; chain patterns in the song editor.

## How audio works on Animux

Animux uses **PipeWire**, which plays the roles of PulseAudio (normal desktop sound) and JACK (professional low-latency audio) at once. Normally you do nothing.

- **Volume and devices**: the speaker icon on the panel, and **PulseAudio Volume Control** (*Sound Engineering → Sound Server Configuration*): choose the output (speakers, HDMI, headphones) and input (microphone) on the *Output Devices*, *Input Devices* and *Configuration* tabs.
- **JACK programs** (Ardour, Hydrogen, Qsynth…) connect to PipeWire's JACK service automatically. If a program cannot find JACK, start it with `pw-jack`, for example `pw-jack hydrogen`.
- **QjackCtl** shows and changes connections between audio programs (the **Graph** button).

!!! tip "Crackling sound while recording"
    Close other programs. In Ardour choose a larger buffer size (512 or 1024 samples). In a virtual machine audio is often unreliable; record on a real computer if you can.

## Sound for animation: tips

- Record dialogue **before** animating, then animate to it (lip sync). Import the WAV in Blender's timeline (*Add → Sound* in the Video Sequencer) or in Pencil2D's sound layer.
- Use **48 kHz WAV** files throughout; it is the film and video standard.
- Free sound effects and music: <https://freesound.org/>, <https://opengameart.org/>, <https://freemusicarchive.org/>. Check each licence.


---
<!-- page: software/upscayl (md/software/upscayl.md) -->
# Upscayl

> Enlarge images 2× to 4× and make them sharper with AI models that run on your own computer, offline.

<div class="factbox" markdown="1">

| Upscayl | |
|---|---|
| Menu | 2D Graphics → Ancillary Tools → Upscayl |
| Version | 2.15.0 |
| Command | `/opt/Upscayl/upscayl` |
| Good for | Beginner |
| Files | PNG, JPEG, WebP |
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 |
| Website | [upscayl.org](https://upscayl.org/) |

</div>


**Upscayl** uses AI models (Real-ESRGAN and others) to make images larger **and** sharper, where normal resizing makes them blurry. Useful for:

- rendering at half resolution and upscaling, to save render time (check the result closely);
- old textures and reference photos;
- concept art and backgrounds.

Everything runs on your computer; no image is uploaded.

![Upscayl: choose an image, a model and the scale, then click Upscayl.](../../images/upscayl.webp)

## Steps

1. Start **2D Graphics → Ancillary Tools → Upscayl** (or type `/opt/Upscayl/upscayl`).
2. **Select Image** (or a folder, with *Batch Upscayl*).
3. Choose an **AI model**: *Upscayl Standard* for photos and renders, *Digital Art* for drawings and anime.
4. Choose the **scale** (2×, 3×, 4×) and the output folder.
5. Click **Upscayl** and wait.

!!! note "Speed"
    Upscayl uses the graphics card through **Vulkan**. With a real AMD, Intel or NVIDIA graphics card it takes seconds. In a virtual machine or without a Vulkan-capable driver it falls back to the slow software renderer (*lavapipe*), and a large image can take many minutes.

For animation frames, upscale the whole **image sequence** folder with Batch mode, then build the video with FFmpeg ([video tools](video-tools.md#ffmpeg-the-five-most-useful-commands)). Check a few frames first: AI upscaling can make small details flicker from frame to frame.

More AI tools (subtitles, background removal, chat models, Stable Diffusion): [AI tools](ai-tools.md).


---
<!-- page: software/ai-tools (md/software/ai-tools.md) -->
# AI tools

> Speech to text and subtitles (Whisper), background removal (rembg), local chat models (Ollama) and Stable Diffusion (ComfyUI), all running on your own computer.

Animux comes with AI tools that run **on your own computer**. Nothing you process is uploaded. Some tools are ready to use; the large ones are downloaded only when you want them.

| Tool | What it does | Ready? | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Whisper** | turns speech into text and subtitles | yes | `animux-whisper` |
| **rembg** | cuts people and objects out of pictures (removes the background) | yes | `animux-rembg` |
| **[Upscayl](upscayl.md)** | makes pictures bigger and sharper | yes, in the menu | — |
| **Ollama** | chat models (like ChatGPT, but offline) | download 1.5 GB | `sudo animux-install-local-ai --ollama` |
| **ComfyUI** | Stable Diffusion: make pictures from text | download 0.5–3 GB, plus a model | `sudo animux-install-local-ai --comfyui` |
| **LTX** in the cloud (Lightricks API) | video **with sound** from text or a picture | LTX account + API key; paid per second of video | `animux-ltx-api` |
| **LTX-2** on your computer | the same, run locally in ComfyUI | NVIDIA card with 24–32 GB; about 40 GB of models | `sudo animux-install-local-ai --ltx-local --cuda` |

!!! note "Internet and space for the first use"
    Every tool downloads its **AI model** the first time you use it (from 70 MB to several GB). After that it works offline. In a [live session](../start/live-session.md) downloads are kept in memory and lost when you switch off; [install Animux](../start/install.md) to keep them.

These tools work from the [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md). Open a terminal in the folder with your files (in the file manager: right-click → *Open Terminal Here*).

## Whisper: speech to text and subtitles

Whisper listens to an audio or video file and writes down what is said. Use it for dialogue transcripts, lip-sync timing sheets and subtitles.

```
animux-whisper dialogue.wav --model small --language en
```

It writes `dialogue.txt`, `dialogue.srt` and other formats into the folder the terminal is in. Video files work too (`scene01.mp4`). Useful options:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--model tiny` / `base` / `small` / `medium` / `large` | bigger = more accurate and slower. `small` is a good start. First download: tiny 72 MB, small 460 MB, large 2.9 GB. |
| `--language en` | the spoken language (`de`, `fr`, `es`, `ja` …). Without it Whisper guesses. |
| `--output_format srt` | only the subtitle file. `txt` = plain text, `all` = every format. |
| `--task translate` | translate the speech into English. |
| `--output_dir subtitles` | where to put the files. |

On the Animux test machine (4 processor cores, no graphics card) the `tiny` model wrote down a 9-second clip in 10 seconds, including the model download. Names it has never heard may be misspelt ("Animux" became "Anomox"), so check the text.

**Subtitles in a film:** load the `.srt` file in [Kdenlive](kdenlive.md) (*Project → Subtitles → Import Subtitle File*), or burn it in with FFmpeg:

```
ffmpeg -i film.mp4 -vf subtitles=film.srt film-subtitled.mp4
```

## rembg: remove backgrounds

rembg cuts out the main subject of a picture and makes the background transparent (a PNG with transparency). Use it for reference photos, collage animation, character turnarounds and compositing.

```
animux-rembg i photo.jpg photo-cutout.png
```

For a whole folder, for example an image sequence:

```
animux-rembg p frames/ frames-cutout/
```

The first time, rembg downloads its model (**about 1 GB**). On the test machine the first picture took two and a half minutes including the download; later pictures take seconds.

!!! tip "Check the edges"
    AI cut-outs can be soft or miss thin parts like hair and fingers. Clean the edge in [Krita or GIMP](gimp-inkscape.md) when it matters. In an image sequence the edge may flicker a little from frame to frame.

## Ollama: chat models on your computer

Ollama runs language models offline: ask for story ideas, dialogue variations, names, or help with commands. Install it once (1.5 GB download):

```
sudo animux-install-local-ai --ollama
```

Then start the Ollama service in one terminal and leave that window open:

```
ollama serve
```

In a **second** terminal, download a model and chat with it (type `/bye` to stop):

```
ollama run llama3.2
```

Models are listed at <https://ollama.com/library>. Small models (1–3 billion parameters, 1–2 GB) answer at reading speed on a normal processor; larger ones need a lot of memory or a graphics card. On the test machine a tiny model (`smollm2:135m`) downloaded and answered within a minute.

## ComfyUI: Stable Diffusion

ComfyUI makes pictures from a text description with Stable Diffusion models. You connect boxes (*nodes*) in your web browser. Install it once:

| Your graphics card | Command |
|---|---|
| NVIDIA | `sudo animux-install-local-ai --comfyui --cuda` |
| AMD (recent) | `sudo animux-install-local-ai --comfyui --rocm` |
| none, or Intel | `sudo animux-install-local-ai --comfyui` (runs on the processor: a picture takes many minutes) |

Start it from **2D Graphics → Ancillary Tools → ComfyUI (Stable Diffusion)** or with `animux-comfyui`. A terminal window opens (keep it open) and Firefox shows ComfyUI at `http://127.0.0.1:8188/`.

ComfyUI does **not** include a model. Download a Stable Diffusion model (a `.safetensors` file, 2–7 GB) from a model site, check its licence, and put it in your own folder:

```
~/ComfyUI/models/checkpoints/
```

Your pictures are saved in `~/ComfyUI/output/`.

!!! warning "Licences of AI models"
    Each model has its own licence, and some forbid commercial use. Read it before you use the pictures in paid work.

## LTX in the cloud: video and sound from text and images

**LTX** by Lightricks makes video clips **with matching sound** (up to 20 seconds, up to 4K) from a text description, or animates a picture, for example a still from your animation. Animux uses the **LTX API**: the video is made on Lightricks' servers, so no special graphics card is needed, but you need an account and it is **paid per second of video** (see <https://docs.ltx.io/pricing>).

1. Create an account and an **API key** at <https://console.ltx.io>, then store the key on Animux (only you can read it):
   ```
   animux-ltx-api key
   ```
2. **Text to video:**
   ```
   animux-ltx-api t2v "A paper boat drifts down a rainy street gutter, close-up, evening light"
   ```
3. **Animate a picture** (it becomes the first frame; describe the motion):
   ```
   animux-ltx-api i2v ~/Pictures/frame-001.png "The character turns her head and smiles"
   ```
   Add `--last ~/Pictures/frame-120.png` to also give the last frame: LTX fills in the movement between the two.

The finished MP4 is saved in `~/Videos/LTX/` (or where `-o file.mp4` says). Useful options:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--model ltx-2-5-fast` | default; `ltx-2-5-pro` gives better quality for a higher price; `ltx-2-3-fast`/`ltx-2-3-pro` are the older models |
| `--duration 6` | length in seconds; `auto` (default, LTX-2.5 only) lets the model choose |
| `--resolution 1920x1080` | also e.g. `1280x720`, `1080x1920` (portrait), `1080x1080` (square, LTX-2.5) |
| `--camera dolly_in` | camera move: `dolly_in`, `dolly_out`, `dolly_left`, `dolly_right`, `jib_up`, `jib_down`, `static`, `focus_shift` |
| `--no-audio` | silent video |

AI agents can use LTX too: `animux-ltx-api mcp` is an MCP server with the tools *text_to_video* and *image_to_video* (see [AI agents](ai-agents.md#4-ltx-video-for-agents)).

On the Animux test machines the command reached the LTX API (it answered with the expected "invalid key" error); making a real video needs your own key and credits.

## LTX-2 on your own computer

With a strong NVIDIA graphics card, LTX-2 can also run **locally** in ComfyUI: no account, no cost per video, nothing leaves your computer.

| | |
|---|---|
| Graphics card | **NVIDIA with 24 GB** (32 GB recommended); on the processor it is far too slow |
| Download | LTX-2.5 (int8): about **40 GB**; LTX-2.3: about 71 GB |
| Licence | LTX-2 Community License: free, also for paid work, for companies below USD 10 million yearly revenue |

1. Install ComfyUI with Lightricks' LTX nodes:
   ```
   sudo animux-install-local-ai --ltx-local --cuda
   ```
2. LTX-2.5 is *gated*: create a free account on huggingface.co, open <https://huggingface.co/Lightricks/LTX-2.5>, accept the licence, then sign in with an access token:
   ```
   /opt/animux/comfyui-env/bin/hf auth login
   ```
3. See what will be downloaded, then download (into `~/ComfyUI/models`):
   ```
   animux-ltx-models
   animux-ltx-models 2.5 --yes
   ```
4. Start ComfyUI (`animux-comfyui`) and open an LTX example workflow from `~/ComfyUI/custom_nodes/ComfyUI-LTXVideo/example_workflows/`.

Versions are pinned by Animux (nodes 1.1.0, fixed model revisions). On the Animux test machine (no graphics card) the installation was tested: ComfyUI loaded all 55 LTX nodes. Making videos locally was not tested, because it needs an NVIDIA card.

## For programmers

The tools live in a Python environment at `/opt/animux/ai-env` (Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.14 for the processor, Whisper, rembg, Hugging Face Hub). Use it for your own scripts:

```
/opt/animux/ai-env/bin/python my_script.py
/opt/animux/ai-env/bin/hf download <model-name>
```

The commands come from the package `animux-ai-tools`.

<!-- page: software/ai-agents (md/software/ai-agents.md) -->
# AI agents in Blender, GIMP, Krita and Inkscape (MCP)

> Let an AI assistant work in Blender, GIMP, Krita and Inkscape through MCP, offline with a local model or with Claude Code; plus Higgsfield and LTX cloud generation.

**MCP** (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI assistant use programs: it can ask Blender what is in the scene and build or change things, paint and edit images in GIMP and Krita, or draw vector shapes in Inkscape. Animux comes with the pieces in the package `animux-mcp`:

| Server | What it is | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **blender** | the official **Blender Lab** MCP server 1.0.3 (Blender Foundation) | scene and file summaries, run code, screenshots, renders, Blender API and manual search |
| **blender-community** | **MCP for Blender** 2.2.4 by Siddharth Ahuja | run code, scene info, viewport look, Poly Haven assets; Animux turns its usage statistics **off** and its safe mode **on** |
| **gimp** | **GIMP MCP** by maorcc (GPL-3.0), for GIMP 3.2 | 79 tools: new images, layers, selections, colour and filters, text, export; run Python in GIMP; off until `animux-mcp gimp on` |
| **krita** | **Krita MCP** by SanSaSane (CC0), for Krita 5.3 | documents, layers, drawing, filters, export; run Python in Krita; off until `animux-mcp krita on` |
| **inkscape** | **inkmcp** 1.0.0 by Shriinivas (AGPL-3.0), for Inkscape 1.4 | create and change SVG elements in the open drawing, document info, PNG preview; run Python (inkex); off until `animux-mcp inkscape on` |
| **animux-guide** | this guide | search and read the guide |
| **higgsfield** | Higgsfield cloud image and video generation | needs a Higgsfield account and uses its paid credits; off by default |
| **ltx-api** | LTX video with sound (Lightricks API), `animux-ltx-api mcp` | needs an LTX API key; paid per second; off by default |
| **ltx-docs** | search the LTX API documentation | off by default |

!!! warning "The assistant can run code in your programs"
    All these bridges let the AI run Python inside Blender, GIMP, Krita or Inkscape **as you**: it can change or delete your work and read and write your files. **Save your work first**, keep backups, and switch a bridge off when you do not use it (`animux-mcp blender off`, `animux-mcp gimp off`, ...). The bridges only accept connections from your own computer. Blender itself recommends using this in a virtual machine or on a computer without sensitive files.

## 1. Switch on a Blender add-on

Only one of the two Blender add-ons can be on at a time (both use port 9876). In a [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md):

```
animux-mcp blender lab          # the official Blender Lab add-on (recommended)
animux-mcp blender community    # or: MCP for Blender
animux-mcp blender off          # switch both off again
```

The official add-on needs *Allow Online Access* in Blender's preferences; `animux-mcp` switches that on (the add-on only listens on your own computer, 127.0.0.1). Then **start Blender**. Check that it is ready:

```
animux-mcp status
```

The last line must say *Blender MCP bridge: listening on 127.0.0.1:9876*.

## 1b. Switch on GIMP, Krita or Inkscape

Each program gets a small plug-in that runs inside it; `animux-mcp` installs it **for your account only** and switches the matching server on in your server list (`~/.config/animux/mcp/servers.json`). Run these as your normal user, not with sudo.

| Program | Switch on | Then |
|---|---|---|
| **GIMP 3.2** | `animux-mcp gimp on` | `animux-mcp gimp start` opens GIMP with the bridge already running (127.0.0.1:9877). Or start GIMP yourself and choose **Tools → MCP → Start MCP Server**. |
| **Krita 5.3** | close Krita, then `animux-mcp krita on` | Start Krita: the bridge starts with it (it uses a secret token stored in your Krita folder). Check it with `python3 /usr/share/animux/mcp/krita/mcp_server.py --selftest`. |
| **Inkscape 1.4** | `animux-mcp inkscape on` | Start (or restart) Inkscape and open a drawing; the AI works on the drawing that is open. It talks to Inkscape through your desktop session (D-Bus). |

`animux-mcp status` shows which bridges are running. Switch one off again with `animux-mcp gimp off` (or `krita off`, `inkscape off`).

These bridges belong to the **new** GIMP 3.2, Krita 5.3 and Inkscape 1.4 from the Animux repository (packages `animux-gimp`, `animux-krita`, `animux-inkscape`); they do not work with the older Debian versions.

## 2a. Offline, with a local model (Ollama)

1. Install Ollama once: `sudo animux-install-local-ai --ollama` (see [AI tools](ai-tools.md#ollama-chat-models-on-your-computer)).
2. Download a model that can **use tools**, for example `ollama pull qwen3:8b` (5 GB; needs about 8 GB of free memory) or, on a small computer, `ollama pull llama3.2` (2 GB).
3. Start the agent: menu **Animux Tools → AI Agent (local, MCP)**, or in a terminal:

   ```
   animux-mcp agent qwen3:8b
   ```

4. Type what you want, for example *"Add a red cube above the monkey and point the camera at it"*. Before each action the agent asks for your OK (**y**). Type `quit` to stop.

Small local models make mistakes with tools; larger models (or a graphics card) work much better.

## 2b. With Claude Code

Claude Code is Anthropic's AI assistant for the terminal. It needs a Claude account (a paid plan or API credits) and the internet. It is Anthropic's program, under their terms, and it updates itself often, so Animux does not ship it: Animux sets it up for you with Anthropic's own installer.

**The easy way:** menu **Animux Tools → Claude Code (AI agent)**. The first time, it asks a few questions and then starts Claude Code. Or, in a [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md):

```
animux-mcp claude-code setup
```

It asks before each step (press Enter for yes):

1. Installs Claude Code from claude.ai (about a minute). The installer's note about *PATH* is taken care of in the next step.
2. Adds Claude Code's folder `~/.local/bin` to your PATH, for new terminals.
3. Switches on the bridges for Blender (official add-on), GIMP, Krita and Inkscape (section 1 and 1b). Close Krita first.
4. Makes the work folder `~/ai-art` (or the folder you name: `animux-mcp claude-code setup ~/my-film`). Claude Code asks once per folder whether you trust it, and never remembers that for your home folder, so work in a folder.
5. Keeps your account's **claude.ai connectors** (Gmail, Google Drive, Calendar, ...) out of Claude Code on this computer, so it cannot read your mail. Then it adds the Animux servers that are switched on (the guide, Blender, GIMP, Krita, Inkscape) to the work folder.

Then start Claude Code from the menu, or with `animux-mcp claude-code start`. The first start asks for a text style, signs you in through your browser, and asks whether you trust the folder: choose **Yes, I trust this folder** (the first answer offered is *No, exit*). Run the setup again at any time, for example after `animux-mcp enable ltx-api`: it updates the servers of the folder. In a live session, everything is gone at power-off, so run it once per session.

**By hand:** install with `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`, add `~/.local/bin` to your PATH, make a folder and go into it, and add the servers there. `animux-mcp claude-code` prints the commands; for example:

```
claude mcp add animux-guide -- /usr/bin/animux-docs mcp
claude mcp add blender -e BLENDER_MCP_HOST=127.0.0.1 -e BLENDER_MCP_PORT=9876 -- /opt/animux/mcp/lab/bin/blender-mcp
claude mcp add gimp -- /opt/animux/mcp/apps/bin/python /usr/share/animux/mcp/gimp/gimp_mcp_server.py
claude mcp add krita -- /usr/bin/python3 /usr/share/animux/mcp/krita/mcp_server.py
claude mcp add inkscape -- /opt/animux/mcp/apps/bin/python /usr/share/animux/mcp/inkscape/extension/inkmcp/main.py
claude mcp list               # each one should say: Connected
```

Then start `claude` in that folder. Start the programs (section 1 and 1b), click back into the terminal and say what you want in plain words, for example *"Use Blender: replace the cube with a monkey on a floor, make her shiny red, and aim the camera at her"*. Claude asks before actions it cannot check; renders in a virtual machine without a graphics card are slow, so ask for a small preview.

## 3. Higgsfield (cloud)

Higgsfield offers 30+ image and video models (and workflows such as product videos and ads) through MCP at `https://mcp.higgsfield.ai/mcp`. It runs in Higgsfield's cloud, needs a Higgsfield account and uses their paid credits; nothing is installed on Animux. With Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add --transport http higgsfield https://mcp.higgsfield.ai/mcp
```

then sign in with `/mcp` inside Claude Code.

## 4. LTX video for agents

With an LTX API key (`animux-ltx-api key`, see [AI tools](ai-tools.md#ltx-in-the-cloud-video-and-sound-from-text-and-images)), agents can make videos with the tools *text_to_video* and *image_to_video*; each call waits until the video is ready and returns the path of the MP4. With Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add ltx-api -- /usr/bin/animux-ltx-api mcp
```

For the local agent: `animux-mcp enable ltx-api` (and `animux-mcp disable ltx-api` to switch it off). Every video costs money, so agents should ask before generating.

## Tested on Animux

On Animux r16 with Blender 5.2.3, both Blender servers listed their tools, read the scene and created an object through MCP; the guide server answered searches.

On Animux r16 (step-39) a test client acting like an AI agent used each bridge in a running program: **GIMP 3.2.6** made a new image, drew an ellipse, added text and exported a PNG; **Krita 5.3.4.1** passed its 9 self-checks, made a document, drew and exported a PNG; **Inkscape 1.4.4** added a circle and text to the open drawing, read the document and returned a PNG preview.

On Animux r16.1 (`_25`, step-44) **Claude Code** 2.1.312 in the live session used all four bridges, each started as described above: a monkey scene with a red material and a Cycles preview in Blender, a sunset poster with three layers in GIMP, a night-sky painting in Krita and a logo in Inkscape. This is the tutorial video *AI agents in Blender, GIMP, Krita and Inkscape*.

On the same live session (step-45), `animux-mcp claude-code setup` (animux-mcp 1.2.0) installed Claude Code 2.1.312, switched on the four bridges and added five servers to `~/ai-art`; `claude mcp list` showed all five *Connected* and none of the account's claude.ai connectors, and the menu entry started Claude Code in that folder.

Animux changes three small things in the upstream code, all checked at build time: GIMP MCP gets one renamed setting for the current MCP library; inkmcp is made to run on the Python 3.8 inside the Inkscape AppImage, starts Inkscape the way the AppImage needs for exports, and keeps its request file in a private folder (`~/.cache/inkmcp`) instead of the shared `/tmp`.

## For programmers and AI agents

- Server list (the usual `mcpServers` format): `/etc/animux/mcp/servers.json`; with your on/off choices applied: `~/.config/animux/mcp/servers.json` (`animux-mcp config` prints it). Switch any server: `animux-mcp enable|disable <name>`.
- Server programs: `/opt/animux/mcp/lab/bin/blender-mcp`, `/opt/animux/mcp/community/bin/mcp-for-blender`, `animux-docs mcp`; GIMP and Inkscape servers run on `/opt/animux/mcp/apps/bin/python` (`/usr/share/animux/mcp/gimp/gimp_mcp_server.py`, `/usr/share/animux/mcp/inkscape/extension/inkmcp/main.py`), the Krita server on `/usr/bin/python3 /usr/share/animux/mcp/krita/mcp_server.py` (standard library only).
- Versions and licences: `/usr/share/animux/mcp/VERSIONS`.
- Headless Blender with the official add-on: `blender --background file.blend --command blender_mcp`.
- See also [For AI agents](../agents/overview.md).

<!-- page: software/storyboard-publishing (md/software/storyboard-publishing.md) -->
# Storyboards, print and PDF

> Plan your film with storyboards in Krita, Blender or Scribus, make an animatic, and lay out posters, scripts and portfolios as PDF.

## Storyboards

A **storyboard** is your film as a comic: one drawing per shot, with notes on action, camera and sound. Three ways on Animux:

| Way | How |
|---|---|
| **Krita** | **File → New → Templates → Comic Templates** (panels ready). Or one image per shot in the *Storyboard* docker (**Settings → Dockers → Storyboard**), which can export a PDF. |
| **Blender** | **File → New → Storyboarding**: draw with Grease Pencil on frames, with a camera per shot. Play it directly as an animatic. |
| **Scribus** | lay out drawn panels with text boxes for dialogue and notes, export PDF for the team. |

## Animatic

An **animatic** is the storyboard timed to the soundtrack: each drawing is shown as long as its shot will last. It shows whether the story works before you animate. Put the drawings and the recorded dialogue in [Kdenlive](kdenlive.md) and adjust the lengths, or use Blender's Storyboarding template.

## Scribus

**Publishing → Desktop Publishing → Scribus** makes page layouts: storyboard sheets, posters, comics, portfolios, festival press kits.

1. **File → New**: page size (A4, Letter, or your own), margins.
2. Draw **image frames** (I) and **text frames** (T), then **File → Import → Get Image / Get Text**.
3. **File → Export → Save as PDF** (choose *PDF/X* for professional printing).

## PDF tools

- **Document Viewer** (Evince) reads PDFs.
- **PDF Arranger**: merge PDFs, reorder, rotate and delete pages by dragging.

<!-- page: software/system-tools (md/software/system-tools.md) -->
# System tools

> Backups with Timeshift, disks with Disks and GParted, burning with K3b, system monitors, virtual machines, containers and remote access.

## Backups

| Tool | Backs up | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Timeshift** (*Digital Asset Managers*) | the **system** (installed Animux) | take a snapshot before big updates; roll back if something breaks |
| a copy to an external disk | your **projects** | drag `~/Projects` to the disk in the file manager, or use the command below |
| **Borg**, **rsnapshot**, **rclone** (terminal) | projects, automatically, also to the cloud | for advanced users |

```
rsync -a --info=progress2 ~/Projects/ /media/$USER/BACKUP/Projects/
```

Timeshift does **not** back up your Home folder by default. That is what the project copy is for.

## Disks

- **Disks** (*System → Disks*): see all disks, check their health (*SMART Data*), format USB sticks, create disk images.
- **GParted** (*System → GParted*): resize and create partitions.

!!! danger
    Both can erase data. Check the disk name and size twice before you click *Format* or *Apply*.

## Burning discs: K3b

**DVD Authoring → Backup → K3b**. *New Data Project* for a backup DVD, *New Video DVD Project* if you already have DVD video files, *Burn Image* to write an ISO to disc.

## Watching the system

| Tool | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Task Manager** (*System*) or `htop` | which programs use processor and memory; end a frozen program |
| `btop`, `glances` | a colourful overview of everything |
| `nvidia-smi` (NVIDIA driver installed) | graphics card use |
| **Psensor** | temperatures. Long renders heat the computer; check that fans work |
| `df -h`, **Disk Usage Analyzer** | free disk space |

## Virtual machines and containers

Animux includes **QEMU**, **Virtual Machine Manager** (*System → Virtual Machine Manager*), **Docker** and **Podman** for running other systems or packaged services (for example a web server for a render farm dashboard). They are for advanced users.

## Remote access

The **SSH** server is installed and enabled on installed systems. From another computer: `ssh your-login@animux-computer`. Useful to start renders on a render node. Change the default live password if a live system is connected to a network you do not trust.

## Security

`ufw` (firewall), `fail2ban`, `rkhunter` and `lynis` are included. On r16 (`_21`) the `fail2ban` service reports an error at start-up (fixed in r16.1, see [Troubleshooting](../help/troubleshooting.md)); it does no harm.

<!-- page: tutorials/first-3d-render (md/tutorials/first-3d-render.md) -->
# Your first 3D render

> In Blender, replace the default cube with a monkey head, give it shiny red paint, add a floor, light it and render a picture. About 30 minutes, no experience needed.

At the end you will have this picture, made by you:

![The finished render: Suzanne, Blender's monkey mascot, in red paint on a grey floor.](../../images/first-render.webp)

You will learn the basics every 3D program shares: **objects, the viewport, materials, lights, the camera and rendering**.

!!! tip "The finished file"
    If you get stuck, download [first-render.blend](../../files/first-render.blend) and open it in Blender (**File → Open**) to compare.

## 1. Start Blender

**Animux → 3D Animation → Modellers → Blender**. Click outside the welcome screen to close it. You see the default scene: a **cube**, a **camera** (the pyramid shape) and a **light** (the dotted circle).

![The default scene.](../../images/blender-01-start.webp)

Try moving the view (this does not change the scene):

| Do | Mouse |
|---|---|
| Orbit around | hold the **middle mouse button** (the wheel) and move |
| Pan | **Shift** + middle mouse button |
| Zoom | turn the **wheel** |

No middle button (laptop)? Use the small coloured axes at the top right of the viewport: drag them to orbit, and use the hand and magnifier icons below them.

## 2. Replace the cube with a monkey

1. **Click the cube** to select it (it gets an orange outline).
2. Press **X** and choose **Delete** (the mouse must be over the 3D view).
3. In the viewport's header click **Add → Mesh → Monkey**. Suzanne appears where the cube was.
4. Make her smooth: **right-click** on her → **Shade Smooth**.
5. Make her rounder: press **Ctrl+2**. This adds a *Subdivision Surface* modifier (you can see it in the **Modifiers** tab, the blue wrench).

![Suzanne, smooth and subdivided.](../../images/blender-02-monkey.webp)

## 3. Add a floor

1. **Add → Mesh → Plane**.
2. Make it bigger: press **S**, type `15`, press **Enter**.
3. Move it down under Suzanne: press **G**, then **Z**, type `-1`, press **Enter**.

The keys **G** (grab), **R** (rotate) and **S** (scale), followed by **X**, **Y** or **Z** and a number, are the fastest way to place things.

## 4. Paint it red

1. Click **Suzanne** again to select her.
2. In the **Properties** editor (right side), click the **Material** tab, the red-and-grey sphere at the bottom of the tab column.
3. Click **New**. A material called *Material* with a **Principled BSDF** is created.
4. Click the white bar next to **Base Color** and choose a red.
5. Set **Roughness** to `0.3` for a shiny paint (0 = mirror, 1 = matt).
6. To see colours in the viewport, switch the shading to **Material Preview**: the third of the four sphere buttons at the top right of the viewport (or press **Z** → *Material Preview*).

![The Material tab with a red base colour; the viewport in Material Preview.](../../images/blender-03-material.webp)

Give the floor a grey-blue material the same way (select the plane, **New**, pick a colour, Roughness `0.6`).

## 5. Light and camera

- **Light**: click the light in the **Outliner** (top right list). In the **Object Data** tab (the green bulb) set **Power** to `2500 W`.
- **Camera**: press **Numpad 0** to look through the camera (or **View → Cameras → Active Camera**). The scene is already framed. To change the view: **View → Navigation → Walk/Fly** or, easier, move the view where you like and press **Ctrl+Alt+Numpad 0** to move the camera there.

## 6. Render settings

1. Click the **Render** tab in Properties (the camera-back icon, second from the top).
2. **Render Engine**: **Cycles**. **Device**: **CPU** (always works).
3. Under **Sampling → Render**, set **Max Samples** to `32` and keep **Denoise** ticked. More samples = less noise but slower.

![Render properties: Cycles, CPU, 32 samples.](../../images/blender-04-settings.webp)

4. In the **Output** tab (the printer icon), check **Resolution**: `1280` × `720`, `100 %`.

## 7. Render!

Press **F12** (or **Render → Render Image**). A new window opens and the picture builds up tile by tile. In a VM or on an older computer it may take a minute.

![The render window with the finished picture.](../../images/blender-05-render.webp)

## 8. Save the picture and the scene

- In the **render window**: **Image → Save As…**, choose `Pictures`, type the name `first-render.png`, click **Save As Image**.
- In the **main window**: **File → Save As…** (Ctrl+Shift+S), make a folder `Projects`, name `first-render.blend`.

!!! warning "Live session"
    In the live session, copy both files to a USB stick before you switch off. See [The live session](../start/live-session.md).

## What next?

- Change the colour, the light, or add a second object (**Add → Mesh → UV Sphere**), and render again.
- Make it move: **[A turntable animation](turntable-animation.md)**.
- Learn more: Blender's manual (*Help → Manual*) and the free courses at <https://studio.blender.org/training/>.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/turntable-animation (md/tutorials/turntable-animation.md) -->
# A turntable animation

> Make Suzanne spin once around in four seconds with two keyframes, then render the animation straight to an MP4 video. About 20 minutes.

A **turntable** shows a model from every side: it turns once around. Studios use turntables to present models. You need the scene from [Your first 3D render](first-3d-render.md) (or download [first-render.blend](../../files/first-render.blend)).

This is the result (4 seconds, 24 frames per second):

<video controls loop muted playsinline width="640" poster="../../images/first-render.webp" src="../../files/turntable.mp4"></video>

The finished file: [turntable.blend](../../files/turntable.blend).

## Keyframes, in one sentence

You tell Blender where an object is at a few moments (**keyframes**), and Blender calculates every frame in between.

## 1. Set the length

At the bottom, in the **Timeline**, set **Start** to `1` and **End** to `96`. At 24 frames per second that is 4 seconds.

## 2. First keyframe: frame 1

1. Make sure the current frame (the blue number in the timeline) is **1**.
2. Select **Suzanne**. In the **Object** tab of Properties (orange square), look at **Rotation Z**.
3. Hover the mouse over the **Rotation Z** field and press **I**. The field turns **yellow**: it has a keyframe on this frame. A diamond appears in the timeline.

## 3. Second keyframe: one turn later

1. Type `97` in the current-frame box of the timeline (one frame after the end, so the loop has no repeated frame).
2. In **Rotation Z**, add 360 to the number that is there (for example `40` becomes `400`) and press **Enter**.
3. Hover over the field and press **I** again.

![The timeline with keyframes; Rotation Z is yellow because it is animated.](../../images/blender-06-keyframes.webp)

Press **Space** to play. Suzanne turns, but she starts slowly, speeds up and slows down again ("ease in, ease out"). For a turntable the speed must be even:

4. Move the mouse over the **timeline**, press **A** (select all keyframes), then **T** and choose **Linear**.

Play again with **Space**: an even, endless spin. Press **Space** to stop.

## 4. Render to a video file

1. Open the **Output** tab (the printer icon).
2. Under **Output**, set the path to `//turntable` (`//` means "in the same folder as the .blend file").
3. Set the **File Format** to **FFmpeg Video** (in Blender 5 first choose the media type **Video**).
4. Under **Encoding**: **Container** `MPEG-4`, **Video Codec** `H.264`, **Output Quality** `Medium quality`.

![The Output tab: resolution, frame range 1–96 and the output path "//turntable". File Format and Encoding are further down; scroll the panel.](../../images/blender-07-output.webp)

5. Lower the **Max Samples** in the Render tab to `16` to make it faster. 96 frames take a while.
6. **Render → Render Animation** (Ctrl+F12). Blender renders frame after frame. When it is finished, the file `turntable0001-0096.mp4` is next to your `.blend` file.
7. Watch it: double-click it in the file manager (it opens in VLC), or **Render → View Animation** in Blender.

!!! tip "Image sequences are safer"
    For real projects, render to **PNG** images instead of a video (File Format **PNG**, path `//frames/turntable_`). If Blender stops at frame 60, you keep frames 1–59 and continue from 60. Join the images into a video with FFmpeg or Kdenlive afterwards ([how](../software/video-tools.md#ffmpeg-the-five-most-useful-commands)).

## Render without opening Blender

Close Blender and render from a terminal; it is faster and you can keep working:

```
blender -b ~/Projects/turntable.blend -a
```

See [Command-line rendering](command-line-rendering.md).

## Next

- Animate other properties the same way: location (a jumping ball), scale, colour (hover over any field and press **I**).
- [A character with MakeHuman](character-makehuman.md).


---
<!-- page: tutorials/character-makehuman (md/tutorials/character-makehuman.md) -->
# A character with MakeHuman

> Create a human character with MPFB inside Blender, give it a skeleton, pose it and set a keyframe, or design it in MakeHuman II and bring it over. About 30 minutes.

Modelling a believable human by hand takes weeks. With **MPFB** (in Blender) or **MakeHuman II** (on its own) you get one in minutes, with a skeleton for animation. See [MakeHuman II and MPFB](../software/makehuman.md) for the background.

## Way 1: MPFB, directly in Blender (recommended)

### 1. Create the human

1. Start **Blender**. Delete the cube (**X → Delete**).
2. Move the mouse over the 3D viewport and press **N**: the **side panel** opens on the right. Click its **MPFB** tab.
3. Open the **New human** section, then **From scratch**, and click **Create human**.

![A new MPFB human in Blender. The side panel (N) is open; its vertical tabs at the right edge are Item, Tool, View, Animation and **MPFB v2.0.18**: click MPFB.](../../images/blender-08-mpfb.webp)

Press **Numpad .** (period) to zoom to the selected human.

### 2. Shape the body

Open **Model** in the MPFB tab. The **Macrodetails** sliders change the whole body: **gender**, **age**, **muscle**, **weight**, **height**, **proportions**. The other groups (head, face, torso, arms, legs) change details. Move a slider and watch the body change.

### 3. Skin, eyes and hair

Open **Apply assets** and pick a **skin**, **eyes**, **eyebrows** and **eyelashes** from its lists. Hair and clothes come from asset packs (see the note on [asset packs](../software/makehuman.md#mpfb-inside-blender)).

Switch the viewport to **Material Preview** (Z → Material Preview) to see the skin.

### 4. Add a skeleton

1. With the human selected, open **Rigging → Standard rig** and click **Add standard rig**. An **armature** (skeleton) appears inside the body, and the body follows it.
2. For more animation controls use **Rigify** instead (*Rigging → Rigify*), then *Generate rigify rig*.

### 5. Pose and animate

1. Click the **armature** (in the Outliner it is called *Human.rig* or similar).
2. Switch to **Pose Mode**: **Ctrl+Tab** (or the mode menu at the top left of the viewport).
3. Click a bone, for example the upper arm, and rotate it: **R**, move the mouse, click.
4. Set a keyframe: press **I** with the mouse in the viewport.
5. Go to frame 24, pose the arm differently, press **I** again. Press **Space** to play.

MPFB can also load ready **poses** and **animations** (*Rigging → Poses* / *Animation*), including Mixamo-compatible animation (*Rigging → Snap to Mixamo*).

## Way 2: design in MakeHuman II, animate in Blender

1. Start **3D Animation → Modellers → MakeHuman 2**, keep the base mesh **fantasy**, and shape the character with the modelling sliders.
2. Save it: **File → Save** as `my-hero.mhm`.
3. In Blender's MPFB tab: **New human → From save file**, choose `my-hero.mhm`.

Or export from MakeHuman II as **GLB** and import it in Blender with **File → Import → glTF 2.0**. That brings the mesh and skeleton, but MPFB's sliders are then no longer available.

![MakeHuman II.](../../images/makehuman2.webp)

## Tips

- Keep characters at real size (a person is about 1.7 m in Blender).
- Save often: **Ctrl+S**.
- For lip sync, MPFB's **Face operations** offer *Load face shape keys* and *Assign Lip Sync shape keys*.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/bouncing-ball-synfig (md/tutorials/bouncing-ball-synfig.md) -->
# A bouncing ball in Synfig

> The classic first animation exercise. Make a ball fall, squash and bounce with waypoints and ease in and out, then export a GIF. About 30 minutes.

The bouncing ball teaches three of the **twelve principles of animation**: **timing**, **slow in and slow out**, and **squash and stretch**. Animux has a finished version as a sample: `/usr/share/animux/samples/synfig/bouncing-ball.sif`.

![The sample bouncing ball open in Synfig Studio.](../../images/synfig.webp)

## 1. A new document

1. Start **2D Animation → Synfig Studio**.
2. **Canvas → Properties** (or the *Canvas MetaData* button): on the **Time** tab set **End Time** to `24` (one second at 24 fps). Click **OK**.

## 2. Draw the ground and the ball

1. Pick the **Rectangle tool** and drag a long, thin rectangle at the bottom: the ground.
2. Pick the **Circle tool**, choose a colour in the toolbox's *Fill colour* box, and drag a circle near the top: the ball.

## 3. Animate the fall and bounce

1. Click the **Animation mode** button at the bottom right of the canvas. The canvas gets a **red border**: from now on every change is recorded.
2. **Frame 0**: the ball is at the top. Select the circle layer, and in **Params** right-click **Origin** → **Add Waypoint** (or simply move the ball a tiny bit).
3. Move the **time slider** to frame **12**. Drag the ball down until it touches the ground. A waypoint appears in the **Timetrack**.
4. Move to frame **24** and drag the ball back to the top.
5. Press **Play** (or drag the time slider). The ball goes down and up.

## 4. Make it feel heavy: slow in and out

A real ball is **slow at the top** and **fast at the bottom**. In the Timetrack, right-click the waypoints at frames 0 and 24 → **Both → Ease In/Out** (slow), and the one at frame 12 → **Both → Linear** (fast, sharp bounce). Play again: it looks much more natural.

## 5. Squash and stretch

At the moment of impact the ball squashes. Add this with a **Scale** or **Stretch** layer above the circle (*Layer → New Layer → Distortions → Stretch*):

- frame 10: amount `1.0, 1.1` (a little stretched while falling fast);
- frame 12: amount `1.3, 0.7` (squashed on the ground);
- frame 14: back to `1.0, 1.0`.

Set the stretch's centre at the ball's bottom.

## 6. Export

**File → Render**: file name `ball.gif`, **Target** `gif`, click **Render**. Or for editing in Kdenlive: target `png` (one image per frame).

From a terminal:

```
synfig ~/ball.sifz -t gif -o ~/ball.gif
```

Turn **Animation mode** off before you continue drawing, and save (**File → Save**, `.sifz`).

## Next

Make the ball bounce several times, lower each time; add a shadow that grows as the ball comes down. Then try a character with **bones** (*Skeleton layer*), see <https://synfig.readthedocs.io/>.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/hand-drawn-pencil2d (md/tutorials/hand-drawn-pencil2d.md) -->
# Hand-drawn animation in Pencil2D

> Draw a short flip-book animation frame by frame with onion skin, play it back and export it as GIF or MP4. About 30 minutes, perfect for beginners and children.

Traditional animation is a series of drawings shown quickly. Pencil2D makes it as easy as a flip book.

![Pencil2D: tools on the left, colours on the right, the timeline with layers at the bottom.](../../images/pencil2d.webp)

## 1. Get ready

1. Start **2D Animation → Pencil2D**. A new project with a **Camera**, a **Vector** and a **Bitmap** layer opens.
2. Click the **Bitmap** layer in the timeline (that is where you draw like on paper).
3. Pick the **Pencil** tool (N) and a dark colour. With a drawing tablet, pressure works automatically.

## 2. Key drawings

Animators start with the **keys**, the most important poses. We will animate a ball jumping across the screen.

1. **Frame 1**: draw the ball on the left, on the ground.
2. Click **frame 7** in the Bitmap layer, then the **+** button (*Add Frame*) above the layers. Draw the ball high in the middle.
3. **Frame 13**: add a frame and draw the ball on the right, on the ground.

## 3. In-betweens with onion skin

1. Turn on **onion skin**: the onion buttons above the timeline (*previous* and *next*). The drawings before and after appear faintly in red and blue.
2. Click **frame 4**, add a frame, and draw the ball halfway between frame 1 and 7: a little lower than half the height (the ball is faster near the ground).
3. Do the same on **frame 10**.

Each drawing is held until the next one: frame 1 shows until frame 3, and so on. That is animating **on threes**.

## 4. Play it

Press **Play** (or **Enter**). Change the speed in the **FPS** box next to the play buttons: `12` is classic for hand-drawn animation. Switch on **Loop** to watch it repeat.

Too jerky? Add more in-betweens (frames 2, 3, 5, 6…) and animate on twos or ones.

## 5. Colour

Pencil2D's **Bucket** (K) fills closed areas. For clean colouring, draw lines on a **Vector** layer: its bucket fill follows the lines exactly, even after you edit them.

## 6. Export

- **File → Export → Movie**: choose **MP4** (for Kdenlive or sharing) or **GIF** (for the web) and the size.
- **File → Export → Image Sequence**: PNG files, the best quality for editing.

Save your project with **File → Save** (`.pclx`).

## Next steps

- Add a **Sound** layer (*Layer → New Sound Layer*) to animate to music or a voice.
- Use the **Camera** layer to pan across a wide background.
- The twelve principles of animation (Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, *The Illusion of Life*) are the best next thing to learn. The [bouncing ball in Synfig](bouncing-ball-synfig.md) teaches the first three.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/krita-animation (md/tutorials/krita-animation.md) -->
# Paint an animation in Krita

> Use Krita's animation workspace to paint a short loop, such as a flickering candle flame, with onion skins, then render it to a video. About 40 minutes.

Krita animates like Pencil2D but with all its painting brushes, so it is good for **painterly effects**: fire, water, smoke, magic. We paint a candle flame that loops.

![Krita's welcome screen.](../../images/krita.webp)

## 1. A new animation document

1. Start **2D Graphics → Bitmap Editors → Krita**.
2. **File → New**: width `1080`, height `1080`, *Create*.
3. **Window → Workspace → Animation**. The **Timeline** (bottom), **Animation** and **Onion Skins** panels appear.
4. In the **Animation** panel set **Frame rate** `12`, **Start** `0`, **End** `11` (one-second loop).

## 2. Background and candle

1. Fill the background layer dark (bucket fill, **F**).
2. Add a layer (**Insert**) named *Candle* and paint the candle body. It does not move, so it needs no frames.

## 3. The flame, frame by frame

1. Add a new layer *Flame*. In the timeline, right-click frame **0** of *Flame* → **Create Blank Frame**.
2. Paint a flame with a soft brush (orange-yellow, brighter in the middle).
3. Turn on the **onion skin** (the light bulb icon on the *Flame* layer in the timeline).
4. Click frame **2**, right-click → **Create Blank Frame**, and paint the flame a little taller and leaning left. Continue on frames 4, 6, 8 and 10 with small changes. Each drawing holds for two frames (animating on twos).
5. Make frame 10 lead back to frame 0, so the loop is smooth.

## 4. Play and adjust

Press **Play** in the Animation panel, and switch on **looping**. Drag frames in the timeline to change the timing.

## 5. Glow

Duplicate the *Flame* layer, put the copy below it, apply **Filter → Blur → Gaussian Blur** (large radius) to each of its frames and set its blending mode to **Add** or **Screen**. The flame now glows.

## 6. Render

**File → Render Animation**:

- **Image Sequence** (PNG): best for editing in Kdenlive;
- **Video**: choose **MP4** and the output file. Krita uses FFmpeg (included). The first time, Krita may ask for the FFmpeg location: `/usr/bin/ffmpeg`.

Save the project as `.kra`.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/stop-motion-webcam (md/tutorials/stop-motion-webcam.md) -->
# Stop motion with a webcam

> Set up a tiny studio, capture a clay or LEGO animation with Stopmotion's onion skin, and turn it into a video with sound.

## Your studio in 10 minutes

| Need | Tip |
|---|---|
| A webcam | any USB webcam; test it first in VLC (*Media → Open Capture Device*) |
| Something to hold it still | a tripod, a clamp, or tape it to a pile of books. **It must not move at all.** |
| Light | close the curtains, use two desk lamps. Daylight changes and makes the film flicker. |
| A stage | a table against a wall; a sheet of paper as background |
| Characters | plasticine, LEGO, paper cut-outs, toys |

## Capture

1. Start **StopMotion Animation → Stopmotion**.
2. **Settings → Preferences → Video Import**: select your camera (`/dev/video0` for the first webcam).
3. Click the **camera** button: the live picture appears.
4. Set **onion skin** to show the last 1–2 frames (the slider in the camera bar).
5. Place your character. Take the first frame.
6. Move the character **a very small step** (a few millimetres), check against the onion skin, take the next frame.
7. Repeat. **12 frames = 1 second** of film at 12 fps.

![Stopmotion.](../../images/stopmotion.webp)

!!! tip "Planning"
    A 10-second scene at 12 fps needs 120 photos. Plan the movement first; count the steps. Moving characters slowly at the start and end of a motion (small steps) and faster in the middle (bigger steps) makes it look natural.

## Check and fix

Press **Play**. Delete bad frames (a hand in the picture!) by selecting them and pressing **Delete**. Use the frame rate setting to change the speed.

## Export

**File → Export → Video**, or export the frames as images and make a video with FFmpeg:

```
ffmpeg -framerate 12 -i frame_%04d.jpg -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 my-film.mp4
```

Add music and titles in [Kdenlive](edit-video-kdenlive.md).

## No webcam?

Use a phone camera on a small stand. Take the photos, copy them to Animux (USB cable or a card reader), and import them in Stopmotion with **Edit → Add frames** (or drag them in), or put them straight into Kdenlive as an image sequence.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/edit-video-kdenlive (md/tutorials/edit-video-kdenlive.md) -->
# Edit your film in Kdenlive

> Put rendered shots, a title and music together on a timeline and export an MP4 ready for YouTube. Uses the turntable video from the earlier tutorial. About 30 minutes.

You need some clips: the `turntable0001-0096.mp4` from [A turntable animation](turntable-animation.md) (or download [turntable.mp4](../../files/turntable.mp4)), and any music file (WAV, MP3 or OGG).

![Kdenlive with the turntable video in the project bin.](../../images/kdenlive.webp)

## 1. Project settings

1. Start **NLV Editors → Kdenlive**.
2. **Project → Project Settings**: choose a profile matching your animation, here **HD 720p 24 fps** (1280 × 720, 24 frames per second). Click **OK**.

!!! note "Always choose the profile first"
    If the profile does not match your clips, Kdenlive offers to change it when you add the first clip. Say **yes** if it suggests the clip's own format.

## 2. Bring in the clips

- Drag files from the file manager into the **Project Bin**, or right-click in the bin → **Add Clip or Folder**.
- For an **image sequence** (frames from Blender, Synfig or Krita), choose the first image and tick **Import image sequence**.

## 3. Build the edit

1. Drag the turntable clip from the bin onto the **V1** track of the timeline.
2. Drag it again so it plays twice in a row (two turns).
3. Click on the timeline to move the playhead; press **Space** to play in the **Project Monitor**.
4. To cut: put the playhead where you want the cut and press **Shift+R**. Delete a part by selecting it and pressing **Delete**.

## 4. A title

1. Right-click the Project Bin → **Add Title Clip**.
2. Type the title (for example *Suzanne Spins*), choose font and size, click **OK**.
3. Drag the title clip onto **V2** above the start of the video. It is shown on top.
4. Fade it: right-click the title on the timeline → **Add Effect → Fade → Fade In** and **Fade Out**.

## 5. Music

1. Drag your music into the bin, then onto the **A1** audio track.
2. Trim it to the length of the video by dragging its end.
3. Fade out at the end: **Add Effect → Fade → Fade Out**.
4. Too loud? Add the **Volume (keyframable)** effect and lower it.

## 6. Export

1. **Project → Render** (Ctrl+Enter).
2. Choose the preset **MP4-H264/AAC**.
3. Set the **Output file**, for example `~/Videos/suzanne-spins.mp4`.
4. Click **Render to File**. The *Job Queue* tab shows progress.

Watch the result in VLC. Upload it, send it, or show it.

## Save the project

**File → Save** writes a `.kdenlive` file. It only refers to your clips; keep the clips where they are (in your project folder) or Kdenlive cannot find them later.


---
<!-- page: tutorials/command-line-rendering (md/tutorials/command-line-rendering.md) -->
# Command-line rendering and batch jobs

> Render Blender, Synfig and POV-Ray without opening them, keep renders running after you log out, render overnight, join frames into a video and convert hundreds of images at once.

Rendering from the [terminal](../desktop/terminal.md) is faster (no window to draw), uses less memory, and can run while you work or sleep. The same commands are what render farms and AI agents use.

## Blender

```
blender -b shot.blend -a                              # the whole animation, as set in the file
blender -b shot.blend -s 1 -e 48 -a                   # frames 1 to 48
blender -b shot.blend -f 1                            # only frame 1
blender -b shot.blend -o //frames/sh010_#### -F PNG -a   # choose output path and format
blender -b shot.blend -E CYCLES -a -- --cycles-device CPU
blender -b shot.blend --python-expr "import bpy; bpy.context.scene.cycles.samples=16" -a
```

- `-b` (background) must come **first**, the `.blend` file next, then the options in order; `-a` or `-f` at the **end** (Blender acts on the options in order).
- `####` becomes the frame number with four digits: `sh010_0001.png`.
- `//` means "relative to the .blend file".

## Keep it running after you close the terminal

```
nohup blender -b shot.blend -a > render.log 2>&1 &
tail -f render.log          # watch progress (Ctrl+C stops watching, not the render)
```

Or use `tmux`: type `tmux`, start the render, press **Ctrl+B** then **D** to leave it running; `tmux attach` brings it back.

## Render overnight, then switch off

```
blender -b shot.blend -a && systemctl poweroff
```

(Make sure the computer will not go to sleep first: [Settings → Power](../desktop/settings.md#power-screen-saver-and-lock).)

## Several shots in a row

```
for f in ~/Projects/my-short/04-shots/sh*.blend; do
    blender -b "$f" -a
done
```

## Use all processor cores, or leave some free

Blender uses every core. To keep the computer usable while rendering, lower its priority: `nice -n 19 blender -b shot.blend -a`. To limit threads: `blender -b shot.blend -t 4 -a`.

## Other programs

```
synfig ball.sifz -t png -o frames/ball.png                  # Synfig: all frames
povray +Iscene.pov +Oframes/f.png +W1920 +H1080 +A -D +KFI1 +KFF96   # POV-Ray: frames 1–96 (clock)
inkscape title.svg --export-type=png --export-width=1920      # Inkscape
openscad -o part.stl part.scad                               # OpenSCAD
gaffer execute -script lighting.gfr -nodes Render -frames 1-24  # Gaffer
```

## Frames into a video

```
ffmpeg -framerate 24 -i frames/sh010_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 sh010.mp4
```

## Convert and check many images

```
mogrify -path small -resize 50% -format jpg frames/*.png      # half-size JPEG copies in ./small
oiiotool frames/sh010_0001.exr -o check.png                   # one EXR → PNG
ls frames | wc -l                                             # how many frames are there?
```

## Check that everything still works

```
animux-selftest blender povray synfig
```

See [the self-test](../help/self-test.md). The [command reference for agents](../agents/command-reference.md) lists the command-line use of every program.

<!-- page: tutorials/short-film-workflow (md/tutorials/short-film-workflow.md) -->
# From idea to finished short film

> The stages of an animated film production and which Animux program to use at each one, with a realistic plan for a first 30-second film.

Every animated film, from a school project to a feature, goes through the same stages. Knowing them helps you choose the right program and avoid redoing work.

<div class="pipeline">
<span>Idea</span><span>Script</span><span>Storyboard</span><span>Animatic</span><span>Design</span><span>Assets</span><span>Animation</span><span>Lighting &amp; render</span><span>Compositing</span><span>Edit &amp; sound</span><span>Export</span>
</div>

## The stages and the tools

| Stage | What you make | 2D film | 3D film | Stop motion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Idea and script** | a one-sentence idea, then a short script | Mousepad, Gedit | | |
| **2. Storyboard** | a drawing per shot | [Krita](../software/krita.md), paper + scanner, Blender's Storyboarding template | same | same |
| **3. Animatic** | storyboard timed with dialogue | [Kdenlive](../software/kdenlive.md) | Blender | Kdenlive |
| **4. Voice recording** | dialogue as WAV | [Audacity](../software/audio.md) | Audacity | Audacity |
| **5. Design** | characters, colours, backgrounds | Krita, [Inkscape](../software/gimp-inkscape.md) | Krita, [MakeHuman](../software/makehuman.md) | clay, paper |
| **6. Assets** | finished characters and sets | Synfig cut-outs, Krita backgrounds | [Blender](../software/blender.md) models, rigs, materials | puppets, sets |
| **7. Animation** | the movement, shot by shot | [Pencil2D](../software/pencil2d.md), [Synfig](../software/synfig.md), Krita | Blender | [Stopmotion](../software/stopmotion.md) |
| **8. Lighting and rendering** | final frames as images | export frames | Blender Cycles/EEVEE, [render farm](../software/flamenco.md) | your photos |
| **9. Compositing** | effects, colour correction | Krita, Blender compositor | Blender compositor, [Gaffer](../software/gaffer.md) | Blender compositor |
| **10. Edit and sound** | the film with music, effects, titles | Kdenlive + [Ardour](../software/audio.md) | same | same |
| **11. Export** | MP4 for the web, high-quality master | Kdenlive, [HandBrake](../software/video-tools.md) | same | same |

## Your first 30-second film: a realistic plan

| Week | Do |
|---|---|
| 1 | Idea (one character, one place, one problem). Script of half a page. Storyboard with 8–12 shots. |
| 2 | Record the voices or choose music. Make the animatic in Kdenlive and watch it ten times. Change what does not work **now**. |
| 3 | Design and build: character, background(s). |
| 4–6 | Animate, shot by shot. Start with the hardest shot. Show it to someone every few days. |
| 7 | Render (overnight), colour, final edit, sound mix, titles and credits. Export. |

!!! tip "Keep it small"
    Thirty seconds is 720 frames at 24 fps. One character and one place is plenty. Finished and short beats long and unfinished.

## Rules that save days

- **One folder per project**, with the [layout studios use](../desktop/files.md#a-folder-layout-for-an-animation-project).
- **Name shots by number**: `sh010`, `sh020`… (leaving gaps lets you add `sh015` later).
- **Render to image sequences** (PNG or EXR), not to video. Edit in Kdenlive.
- **Lock the frame rate** (24 or 25 fps) at the start and use it everywhere.
- **Back up** to an external drive every day.
- **Test render small** (25–50 % resolution, few samples) before the final render.

## Credits and licences

If you use music, sounds, fonts or models made by others, check that their licence allows it, and credit them. CC0 means free for everything; CC-BY means free with credit.


---
<!-- page: help/self-test (md/help/self-test.md) -->
# The self-test and sample scenes

> Check in a few minutes that every renderer and the main programs work on your computer, read the results, and use the sample scenes to learn.

**Animux Tools → Animux Self-Test** renders a small scene with every renderer, opens the most important file formats and checks that the main programs start. It takes 2–10 minutes.

![The self-test result in VirtualBox: 29 passed, 0 failed.](../../images/vbox-selftest.webp)

## Reading the results

| Result | Means | Do |
|---|---|---|
| **PASS** | the program ran and produced a correct result | nothing |
| **FAIL** | the program is installed but did not work | open the log file named in the line (see below) |
| **SKIP** | not installed, or this processor is too old for it | "this processor has no SSE4.2/AVX": see [Requirements](../start/requirements.md) |

All pictures, files and logs are kept in **`~/animux-selftest/<date-time>/`**; the menu entry opens that folder at the end. `summary.txt` there has the result list. Attach that folder when you [ask for help](getting-help.md).

## The tests

| Test name | Program | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| `blender` | [Blender](../software/blender.md) | Cycles renders a small scene |
| `apps` | [MakeHuman II](../software/makehuman.md) | the program and its Qt libraries load |
| `povray` | [POV-Ray](../software/renderers.md) | renders samples/povray/animux-spheres.pov |
| `appleseed` | [appleseed](../software/renderers.md) | renders the bundled helloworld project |
| `luxcore` | [LuxCoreRender](../software/renderers.md) | renders samples/luxcore/render.py |
| `mitsuba` | [Mitsuba 3](../software/renderers.md) | renders samples/mitsuba/render.py |
| `pbrt` | [pbrt-v4](../software/renderers.md) | renders samples/pbrt/animux-spheres.pbrt |
| `gaffer` | [Gaffer](../software/gaffer.md) | Cycles render from a Gaffer node graph |
| `usd` | [OpenUSD tools (usdview, usdcat …)](../software/pipeline-formats.md) | reads samples/usd/animux-scene.usda, writes .usdc |
| `alembic` | [Alembic tools (abcls, abctree …)](../software/pipeline-formats.md) | lists samples/alembic/animux-cube.abc |
| `exr` | [OpenEXR and OpenImageIO tools](../software/pipeline-formats.md) | converts PNG to EXR and reads the header |
| `ocio` | [OpenColorIO tools](../software/pipeline-formats.md) | validates samples/ocio/config.ocio |
| `vdb` | [OpenVDB tools](../software/pipeline-formats.md) | makes a level-set sphere and reads it back |
| `flamenco` | [Flamenco](../software/flamenco.md) | manager and worker start |
| `farmerjoe` | [Farmerjoe](../software/flamenco.md) | the Perl script compiles |
| `opentoonz` | [OpenToonz](../software/opentoonz.md) | renders samples/opentoonz/animux-lines with tcomposer |
| `synfig` | [Synfig Studio](../software/synfig.md) | renders frame 12 of samples/synfig/bouncing-ball.sif |
| `apps` | [DJV](../software/video-tools.md) | the program starts |


The `apps` test also checks that MakeHuman 2, DJV, Avidemux and Cinelerra-GG start.

## From the terminal

```
animux-selftest                 # everything
animux-selftest --list          # list the test names
animux-selftest blender povray  # only these
animux-selftest --open          # open the results folder at the end
```

The exit code is 0 when nothing failed, 1 otherwise, so scripts and [AI agents](../agents/overview.md) can use it as a health check.

## Sample scenes

**Animux Tools → Animux Sample Scenes** opens `/usr/share/animux/samples`:

| Folder | File | Open or run with |
|---|---|---|
| `povray/` | `animux-spheres.pov` | menu *Renderers → POV-Ray*, or `povray +Ianimux-spheres.pov +O/tmp/out.png +W800 +H600` |
| `blender/` | `turntable.py` | `blender -b -P turntable.py -- /tmp/out.png` |
| `synfig/` | `bouncing-ball.sif` | Synfig Studio (**File → Open**), or `synfig bouncing-ball.sif -t gif -o /tmp/ball.gif` |
| `mitsuba/` | `render.py` | `animux-vfx-python render.py /tmp/out.exr` |
| `luxcore/` | `render.py` | `animux-vfx-python render.py /tmp/out.png` |
| `gaffer/` | `render.py` | `gaffer env python render.py /tmp/out.exr` |
| `pbrt/` | `animux-spheres.pbrt` | `pbrt --outfile /tmp/out.exr animux-spheres.pbrt` |
| `usd/` | `animux-scene.usda` | `usdview animux-scene.usda` |
| `alembic/` | `animux-cube.abc` | Blender: *File → Import → Alembic*; `abcls -r animux-cube.abc` |
| `ocio/` | `config.ocio` | `ociocheck --iconfig config.ocio` |

The sample files are read-only. Copy one to your Home folder before changing it: `cp -r /usr/share/animux/samples ~/samples`.

More examples: `/usr/share/povray-3.7/scenes` (hundreds of POV-Ray scenes), `/opt/animux/gaffer/resources` (Gaffer), `/opt/animux/appleseed/examples` (appleseed), and the tutorial files on this guide: [first-render.blend](../../files/first-render.blend), [turntable.blend](../../files/turntable.blend).
